subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, July 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickersgill (for Mr. Lapointe) for the second reading of Bill No. 351, to amend the Post Office Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have read the remarks of the genial parliamentary assistant and others who spoke last night in this debate, and I find that I misheard one or two of them. There is no necessity for me to take up the time of the house in continuing the debate now. I shall have certain questions to ask when we get into committee.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Transfer of contract.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister one or two questions in connection with this matter, particularly in view of the fact that he has stated that this amendment merely legalizes what has been done over a period of years. I should like to ask him how many cases there have been during the last five years, year by year,


where transfers have been made from the holders of contracts during the period of the contracts, in each case what was the remuneration given or provided for under the tender; and was there any increase in the amount paid in respect of the contract in consequence of the assignment, transfer or substitution of another person in the place of the original tenderer? If the (parliamentary assistant could give that information it would pretty well cover the situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have not the figures for the five-year period, but foi the year ending September 30, 1954, there were 303 transfers made of contracts under $1,000 and 162 of contracts over $1,000. In no case was there any increase in the price. That is one of the conditions of the amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: I have learned that the minister has received from time to time certain requests respecting an extension of letter boxes in certain towns from which rural routes emanate. I was wondering whether or not any consideration has been given to the thought that in such areas and towns where we have a number of rural routes operating from a central office and they have no letter carrier system, letter carrier boxes be placed in those towns and it be embodied in the contract that it include the picking up of letters from those boxes to be taken to the central post office for delivery.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: If I understood properly the question of the hon. member for New Westminster, I think he refers to letter boxes for the receipt of letters being mailed. Is that correct?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Generally speaking the
policy is that the letter boxes are installed in areas where there is a letter carrier service, and they are not installed where there is no letter carrier service and where people go to the post office anyway. There are exceptions to these rules when the exigencies of the service, if I may use that expression, make it justifiable. As a rule, a rural mail contractor who does the delivery to the rural mail boxes on that route will usually have included as part of his contract the picking up of the mail in that letter box. Of course if in so doing he increases the length of his route, he should be compensated accordingly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
The question resolves itself in this way, however, in so far as certain of these towns from which rural routes emanate are concerned. Some of them are quite large, but they are not large enough for a letter carrier system. The suggestion is made that

the outlying districts might have letter receiving boxes, so that when the rural route carrier comes by, he merely stops, picks up the mail and takes it to the post office, thereby saving citizens a long walk from the outskirts of the town into the post office for that particular purpose.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: I know that is done in some areas. As applications are made at various localities, they are studied in order to find out whether such a service can be given without increasing the cost of the contract or the length of the route the contractor would have to cover.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
This slight amendment simply requests something that apparently the department has been practising for years, and I have noticed it being done; but I have noticed also on one or two occasions that a contract was transferred to someone who, in the opinion of the people in the district, was not nearly as capable or as responsible as the original contractor.
My question is this. What does the department do to make certain that a person to whom a contract is transferred has satisfactory equipment, has the capacity and the ability, and has the same bonding as the original contractor?
In addition, in order to avoid the minister having to rise twice, I am going to ask another question. Do the inspectors emphasize what is the responsibility of a person who signs a bond for one of these contractors?
I remember speaking to an aged clergyman in my district once when there was some possibility of the contractor failing in his obligation, and when he realized what he might be responsible for he nearly had a heart attack. He did not understand what he had signed. I think something should be done to inform the person who signs a bond what are his responsibilities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
The
departmental officials study the case of the individual to whom the contract may be transferred just as carefully as they do the case of the original contractor. It is up to the departmental officials to be satisfied that he is capable and can supply the necessary equipment, the bondsman and so on.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: That process is all gone through again?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Yes. As far as the bond is concerned, I do not know about your friend the aged clergyman, but I would hate to think he would sign a bond without having read it very carefully. Attached to each contract is a bond, of which I have a copy here, and I think he can tell
Post Office Act
from this that he is responsible for operating the route should the original contractor default in any way.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: I think the department has run into several cases of that sort where people have signed these bonds. I believe something should be done to draw to the attention of the person who signs the bond what they are responsible for and not just leave it to them to read the fine print in the contract.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: I should like to ask a question or two. Does this clause apply to any contracts other than rural carrier contracts and, if so, what other contracts?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
This section applies to any contract. It says:
The Postmaster General may . . . substitute another person for the contractor under any contract for the conveyance of mail . . .
That would include rural routes, suburban services, side services, stage services, city services and so on; any contract for the conveyance of mail.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: I was looking at this from the standpoint of the rural carriers. What is the average cost of calling for tenders where you have to post notices for three weeks, when a contract runs out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
At
the moment I do not know what is the actual cost of the calling of the tenders, but I certainly could find that out and let the hon. member know. However, I can say that the cost of the contracts that were transferred during the last year that we transferred contracts was considerably less than the amounts we were receiving in the form of tenders that were called for the new contracts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: In transferring a contract from one rural mail route contractor to another contractor when the term of the contract runs out, has it been the practice of the department to make the arrangements without calling for tenders?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
No
When a contract is transferred it is transferred because in some cases the original contractor has died and his estate wishes to have it transferred to the son or widow, or in other cases because the contractor may have moved from the village or may have sold his store or farm; but when the four-year term has expired and the contract runs out, tenders are then called.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is the point. It looks to me as though the last two lines of the section permit a change in that principle. If the minister or the parliamentary assistant

Post Office Act
can assure the house that there is no intention under this bill to renew a contract with the party with which the arrangement has been made without calling tenders, then I would be quite happy with it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
am sorry; I must have misunderstood the first part of your question. The latter part of this amendment says:
. . and the provisions of this act apply to the person so substituted as though he were the original contractor.
You will remember that when you were speaking last night you said that the system we have been following for some time had been very satisfactory and you hated to see it changed. You may not have used those exact words but I believe that was the gist of your comments. As reported at page 5594 of Hansard you said this:
-which has otherwise been a good one, namely the tender system, subject to renewal for the remainder of the term of the contract.
What we are really asking for is this. We are asking through this amendment to be permitted to carry on what has been done ever since confederation. The amendment is being introduced as I mentioned last night, owing to some question having arisen in the mind of one of the legal experts in the Department of Justice, who questioned whether the act was worded in such a way that we did have permission to do that, even though in the contract which every contractor signs there is section 27, which says:
The said contractor shall not have it in his power to transfer his interest in this contract without the special written sanction of the Postmaster General.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
That fairly well answers the question, except that to my mind this act leaves it open, under section 31. That will be new. I presume that now you are going to introduce an amendment, you will make the present section 31 subsection 1 and this amendment will be subsection 2. So we will say under subsection 1 of section 31 as it is now the department may renew a contract without calling for tenders if they consider it in the interests of the service, and the service provided has been satisfactory.
When this bill is passed do you consider that you will have the power to do that? We will say that A gives up a contract; he dies or he moves away and you arrange that the contract is taken over by B. B carries it on for the remainder of the term, whether it is two years, three years or whatever it may be. At the end of the term of that contract do you feel that, under this act, you will be able to renew that contract under section 31 as it now stands, without calling

for tenders? I think you can. If so, and if the department has that in mind, I should like to ask the minister to consider an amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
The
transferee has exactly the same rights as the original contractor.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
As far as I am
personally concerned, I should like to say that I do not like this amendment. It seems to me that it leaves it open to something; I was going to use the word "skulduggery" but I suppose that "indiscretion" would be the better word. It appears to me that when a person has a contract and then, for some reason or another, decides to forgo that contract and so advises the department and makes a recommendation, the department may or may not act upon that recommendation. But at the end of that four-year period when tenders would ordinarily be called, this puts the others in that community who desire to tender on that contract in an extremely embarrassing position.
It is embarrassing to this extent. They are at a great disadvantage to start with because this other fellow already has the advantage of having concluded that former contract. It goes almost without saying that when tenders are finally called, the government would favour the one who had the contract. In that sense it does not leave itself open to a free and competitive form of tender. When the department receive these new tenders they look them over, but they do not necessarily have to take the lowest tender. They look them over and say, "Well, now, this fellow has been carrying on for the last four years under the original contract, and we see no reason why he should not be given the new contract". People who are tendering under those conditions are at a very decided disadvantage.
I cannot see, either, why the department should not call for tenders when the original contractor decides to terminate his contract. There is no great expense attached to it. It is a routine procedure with the department, and surely it would take no time and practically no expense to call for tenders again. This would leave it open to everybody, and everybody would have an equal opportunity. I say again that the man who is recommended by the original contractor has a decided advantage over all the other tenderers when the four-year period is up and tenders are called again. The very fact he has given some service may lead the department to say, "Well, his services have been satisfactory and we do not know anything about this other fellow, so we will let him carry on for another four years."

I do not think that should be permitted. It seems to me the department itself should be very eager to get out of that position where doubt is cast upon the department in this regard. I think they should call for tenders and give everybody an equal and fair opportunity to offer their services and have no embarrassment attached to it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: On the same point exactly, Mr. Chairman, it has occurred to me to ask if under this act there could be collusion between the former contractor and someone to whom he desired to give that contract. I mean, almost at the expiry of the old contract the original contractor could make an arrangement with his friend, and so long as that person was satisfactory to the department he would be allowed to carry on. It seems to me if tenders were called it would avoid a great deal of the criticism of the hon. member who has just spoken.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
the original contractor requests a transfer, and if the transfer is made it is only made if the departmental officials who have checked on the matter feel he is capable of carrying on and giving good service. Then if at the end of the contract period he is giving good service and there are no undue complaints in the area, it is automatically renewed.
So far as the part about calling for tenders is concerned, I may say that the contract is always awarded to the lowest tenderer, except in a rare case when on checking the department finds he is not capable of carrying out the contract. I know of a case that happened in my own riding. A gentleman tendered for the contract and said he could carry it out. He said he had a car, but the departmental officials found that while he had a car, unfortunately it was minus wheels, a starter and a generator. He had no credit with which to get a car and he could not get any bondsmen. He did submit a tender.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Is it a fact that the department always accepts the lowest bid? I do not think that is so, because there may be a situation where a man puts in a bid when he knows he is not going to make very much out of the mail contract. It may be that he has another business and he may say, "Well, I will have enough people coming to my store that it will more than offset any loss I have on the delivery of mail." In that case his bid may be very low. I do not thinfr it is always the practice of the department to accept the lowest bid.
Then there is another case. Suppose the original contractor recommends someone who is not satisfactory to the minister or to the department, then tenders would have to be
Post Office Act
called. Why does the department not call for tenders in the first place? I would think there would be many instances where that would occur. I do not think the department is going to save itself much trouble, and I can see where this would lead to a lot of dissatisfaction and questionable practices. I do not think it should be allowed to continue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
The
contract is awarded to the lowest tenderer if he is capable of performing the work; that always happens. I gave an extreme case that occurred in my constituency. If a man believes people will cut in he tenders low and the contract is awarded to him. As far as the system itself is concerned, as I mentioned two or three times this system has been in vogue since 1867, since confederation, and we have had a lot less trouble by using this method. Those of us who represent rural or partially rural constituencies realize it is very difficult to find people who are interested. Sometimes a local contractor has to give it up and through a personal friendship he is able to find someone to carry it on. Sometimes we call for tenders in these rural areas and we receive no tenders, and we have to call for tenders two or three times.
To return to your main point, the tender is awarded to the lowest tenderer.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: Is there any reason why the original contractor has anything to do with who his successor shall be, except that I think you stated that it saved trouble for the department? What is the idea of having the original contractor interested in his successor?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
I
think a brief answer to that, Mr. Chairman, is that very frequently the original contractor may have served for some years; he has equipment and he knows the route and sometimes through a personal friendship he is able to make an arrangement and transfer his equipment to someone who is willing to carry on.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: From what you state I gather it is virtually a family contract which would exclude others.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Does the original contractor
contact the department before making the transfer, or does he just quit the job and say that he is leaving. What obligation does he have toward the department, if any? He has to make application to the department for the transfer and I think he makes his recommendation. What does the excuse have to be; sickness or bankruptcy or just his whim to give it up? Has he any responsibility?

Post Office Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
In
the vast majority of cases the contractor has died and his route is transferred to the widow. Most of the cases are like that. There are also cases where the man sells his farm or business and wants to move away, or perhaps for some other reason. There are very few cases where the man wants to give it up because of some whim.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, these mail carriers become more than mere mail carriers, they become part of the community and do a great many favours for people other than just carrying the mail. In the case of a person moving away or quitting his job or dying and a new man taking over, I think that should be by contract and the lowest tenderer should get it providing his qualifications are all right. I have known some cases where in advertising for a mail carrier, the qualifications were probably equal and the prices came within $10 to $15 of each other, whoever handled the patronage for the Liberal government in the area got the job.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: And it should have been a Conservative.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
As far as contracts are concerned, if a man is doing his job satisfactorily I do not think the job should be put up for tender when the four-year term is up. That man should have a renewal without any tender whatsoever until such time as he wants to quit himself or until he is too old to carry on. Putting these things up for tender every four years creates a lot of ill feeling within the area, and frequently you get a carrier who is not as good as the previous one. This keeps it within the patronage system, when you renew the contract of a man who is capable and doing the job well.
In my riding last year there was one mail carrier's route put up for tender for no reason at all. He had a petition signed by every box holder on the route, which was sent to the department, but despite this his job went up for tender and was given to another man for the sake of $10. Probably the other man knew how much to tender less than the other fellow; I don't know about that. I think the more you get away from contracted jobs the better it will be for the mail service, the post office department and everyone concerned; but in the case of a new man coming on or a new route being established, then it should be handled by tender.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the point involved here is, I think, a point of principle. I object to the last two lines of the bill because I am satisfied, as the hon. member

for Victoria (Ont.) has said, that some person can get a mail contract who has never tendered.
I am quite in sympathy with the department making arrangements to carry on for the remainder of a term; I think that is good business. As I said last night, I think it is good business to retain the tender system because it has worked very well; but under these two lines in this bill you are inserting the thin edge of the wedge whereby the tender system may disappear.
This is designed to make legal what the department has been doing in the past. As I understand it, the department had not been going beyond making arrangements for the remainder of a contract term. I would be quite willing to have that done; but when that term runs out then I think tenders should be called for that particular contract, because a new person is entering the field and I do not think it is in the interests of the public to handle it in any other way. I think it is putting too much responsibility on the district superintendent or whoever looks after this.
I believe there would be far less fault found if you were to open it to tenders and give the people a chance. As I understand it, it does not cost very much to call for tenders. If we cut out the last two lines of this bill I think the department will have succeeded in accomplishing under this bill what they desire. In other words they will be legalizing the things they have been doing, which I am quite in favour of them doing.
This bill goes further than that. This bill is going to interfere with the principle of permitting a new carrier to get his job under the old tender system. It permits me or someone else to take over from some other person, keep the job for a few months under an arrangement with the department, and have that contract continued from four years to twenty years, with a raise in pay every period under section 33 as amended in 1953, and keep it to myself as long as I render good service.
That may work all right, but we are taking away from the people the right to have a chance to get that job, and I do not agree with that. I am going to suggest, therefore, that the minister consider an amendment, unless he is able to point out to me that the last two lines are important. I move:
That clause 1 of Bill No. 351 be amended by striking out all the words after the word "agree" in line eleven, and in lieu thereof add the following:
"but such substitution shall be only for the remainder of the term of the contract."

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
In view of the answer given by the parliamentary assistant just now, i1

seems to me that where one of these cases arises through the death of the contractor, provision should be made in the bill to take care of such a situation. The clause reads in part:
-that no additional expenditure is involved, substitute another person for the contractor for the conveyance of mail, if the contractor and the person to be so substituted agree.
If one of the parties is dead how can he agree? I think that is where the trouble would start.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: The answer is that it is usually some member of the family of the deceased who is ready to take over.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: It does not say so.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: That is done in order that the contract may remain within the estate. There is generally a member of the family who is willing to take over the contract.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: That should be stated in the bill.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext: It is not necessary.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
* In my submission this is a bad bill, in that the government is now practically doing away altogether with the calling of tenders. In the case of almost any contract, if the original contractor does not wish to renew at the end of four years all he has to do within the last two months of the term of the contract is to say that he is going to give up the contract and is recommending so and so. That will be done in a great many cases and the government will not have to call tenders for any of these rural mail routes. The government is just leaving this thing wide open to patronage and everything else.
I think that is a terrible thing to have happen and I do not think this bill should be allowed to pass. The government will be put in the position of having to call tenders for only a few contracts, because in many cases within two months of the expiration of the contract, if the original contractor does not want to carry on he will simply recommend somebody else. No tenders will be called for the new contract, and the same thing can be done time after time. There will be no need for the department to call for tenders and we will be going back to the patronage system. I am not saying they will do that, but I do contend that this would add to that type of practice.

Post Office Act
of contract from one person to another represents only 3-6 per cent of all contracts. I have no doubt that the hon. member is familiar with the manner in which these contractors do their work. I am sure he knows how these contractors handle their responsibilities, and he knows perfectly well that most of the contractors make this a personal job. They give most of their time to it. On reading Hansard I noticed that during the course of the debate one hon. member made reference to the long and reliable service which is given by some of these rural mail contractors. I think the same condition exists in all our rural communities, and those of us who represent rural communities are aware of that.
It may be that a contractor has been doing this work for many years and has rendered good service to the public. In many cases it is the contractor's only occupation. As was mentioned, in the case of the death of a contractor, in many cases the only people who are familiar with the work are the contractor's family, who very often have done the work for the contractor. By making this transfer a continuity of efficiency in the handling of rural mail is possible. There is nothing new in the practice which this amendment seeks to legalize. As was mentioned before, it has been done ever since confederation, and all we are doing is making sure that the act provides for the continuation of this practice.

One point which should not be forgotten is that when such transfer is made, the department must make sure that the person who takes over the execution of the contract for the remainder of the period is bound by the Post Office Act in the same manner as the original contractor. In other words, he must be under the authority of the Postmaster General in the same manner as was the original contractor. -and the provisions of this act apply to the person so substituted as though he were the original contractor.

It would seem to me, if this practice was carried out in 3 per cent of the cases when, it turns out, it was not even legal, after we legalize it the practice may become more widespread. After all, if this bill is passed the rural mail carrier- I am thinking t>f him especially-is in the position that his contract becomes almost part of his estate, because as long as he gives satisfactory service it will be extended indefinitely.
I think that is a good policy if a man is giving satisfaction. But when he wants to give up his contract all he has to do is give it up short of the date of termination, and then he has the privilege of recommending a successor to himself. Then that successor in turn is in the same position as the original contractor. As long as he gives good service he can carry it on for the rest of his working life if he wants to. In that way the mail contracts can be handed on from generation to generation without ever being put up for tender.
It seems to me that while at the present time it may not be a practice that will apply generally, nevertheless we are making it legal for a practice to creep in whereby mail contracts are something to be inherited, not to be won by submitting the lowest tender.

I have been opposed to the tender system ever since I have had any interest in the rural mail carriers' problems. There is no other employee handling Her Majesty's mail that has to do this work by public tender. I think the public tender system is very vicious, and I believe the amendment that was made in 1953 did something to equalize the pay of the rural mail carriers and has done a good deal to restore some confidence and equity among the rural mail people themselves.
Under the 1953 amendment a tender can be called and an adjustment in pay can be made after two years, or only once during the life of the contract. That situation is not very equitable, because since the 1953 amendment a rural mail carrier who may only be a year or a year and a half from the expiration of the contract may apply for an increase in pay but he cannot have any further adjustment during that period, and he must renew before he can ask for another increase. Consequently he cannot ask for another increase
Post Office Act
for two more years. Therefore the situation at the present time is that it is possible for one person to get an increase in pay in a little over two years while another person would have to wait probably four years. Of course I appreciate that would be taken care of after everybody had renewed and all were in the same boat.
However, to come back to the tender system again, I think the quicker we get away from that system and adopt some other system the better it will be. I am not going to suggest for a minute that the matter should be left entirely in the hands of the Post Office Department and whatever government may be in power at the time, because a lot of political patronage could creep in under those conditions. Nevertheless I do think that the public tender system should be done away with at an early date. The awarding of contracts, rather than being done by public tender, could come under the civil service commission or some other body. Under the present system a person can apply by public tender and ask for an increase in two years' time, and it it quite possible that somebody who wanted to get a particular route could tender at much below the regular price accepted across the board and then ask for an increase in two years and under the present act have his pay increased by the officials to the average across the board.
I cannot see any danger in this amendment. As the Postmaster General has said, it is just making something legal that has been done for a long time. Finally, may I say that to my knowledge I am quite certain that in Ontario particularly there has not been any political patronage.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
I quite agree that the amendment as worded by the hon. member for St. Paul's would have the exact effect that the member who proposed the previous amendment wanted to achieve. In fact, when I was answering the remarks of the hon. member for Prince Albert I said I could have thought of an amendment which would have attained his end and would have been more simple. However, I regret to say that we cannot accept the amendment, and there is one reason I want to mention which has not been mentioned up to now.
It has been the experience of the department that in most cases the transferee, the new contractor, the person who is willing to take over the contract, will not accept the transfer of the contract and assume the obligations of the original contractor unless he is put in the position of having all the rights of the original contractor. He will not take over for a short period of only six months, eight months or even two years without having some assurance that if he performs his work satisfactorily he will have the same privileges as the original contractor. Therefore when such a situation arises the department has to enter into temporary arrangements. The officials of the department go into the locality and try to find someone who is willing to carry on for the balance of the contract.
It is all very nice to say that the sureties under the original contract are bound, but it may be that they are not in a position to carry out their obligation. There is quite a bit of difference between being able to enforce a contract in so far as the persons who signed as sureties are concerned and making sure that the people get good service which, after

all, is what we have in mind. Therefore we have to go about and make temporary arrangements, and it has been the experience over quite some years, I might say without exception, that these temporary arrangements are very costly to the department precisely because the person who is willing to enter into such arrangements knows that the duration will be very short. Therefore very often the balance of the contract will have to be executed at twice the cost of the original contract or what it would be if we simply transferred the contract as has been the practice in the past. We try to avoid these temporary arrangements as much as possible because of the high, uneconomic cost of such operations.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TRANSFER OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
In view of the minister's unwillingness to accept the amendment, and I thought from his earlier remarks that he would, I should like to say a word or two about this section. The minister has referred to 31 per cent of the contracts being transferred by this substitution method in the course of a year. As I understand it, these are four-year contracts, and if that is the case does that not mean that 12 per cent or more of the contracts in force are affected? In any event, it seems to me that if there is a diffidence on the part of some new contractor to come in and fill the unexpired term the proper course, if it is not worth while for the person to do that, is to call for a new contract in the usual way.
Let there be no mistake that the effect of this section, as has been said, is to make it unnecessary to call for tenders. A man can come into a mail delivery contract by substitution under this clause and at the end of the unexpired term his contract can be renewed just as though he had been the original contractor. He could go on then for a number of terms and serve in this capacity without ever having tendered.
This change would make it possible, if it were desired to do so, to bring about a situation in which a good proportion of the contractors in the country were serving without ever having tendered as required by the act. If it is desired to abolish the tender system, why not do it and amend that provision of the act? Let us not approach it through any back door. I think it is clear that this is a back door which could be used for the purpose of permitting a man to enter as a substitute first without having to tender, and then permitting the renewing of the contract without him having to tender, and that process could go on indefinitely.
On that account, as has been stated already, I object to this clause, as do many of us, and shall oppose it unless the amendment is put

in which keeps the tender system or brings it into effect when the unexpired term of the present contract is up for renewal.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in support of what the minister has just said. I presume hon. members who have spoken are thinking in terms of the situations that arise on the mainland where the mail contractor carries the mail from the train to the post office; in other words, he brings the mail from the post office to the train, takes the incoming mail and brings it back. I do not know how lucrative these jobs are on the mainland and how much competition there is for them, but I can assure hon. members that in my province they are not very lucrative and that it is extremely difficult to get people to take them at all.
In Newfoundland, of course, we have an entirely different situation because most of our people live in communities scattered around the coast line, and the mail is brought by a coastal boat. You therefore have three kinds of contractors. You have one contractor who meets the ship at the wharf at the port of call and carries the mail from the wharf to the post office. He had previously brought the mail down to the wharf when the steamer entered the harbour. He picks up the incoming mail and carries it back.
That is one type. Then you have another situation where a carrier brings the mail from one settlement to the port of call. That is an extremely difficult situation. If the port of call, for instance, is A and the community is B which is, say, 10 miles away, the courier in community B very often has no idea at all when the coastal ship will arrive at the port of call A. He must take the mail there in time to catch the ship. That very often means that he must go several hours ahead of time, because after six o'clock the telegraph offices are closed, and he does not know whether or not that ship is going to come during the night. Hence he is obliged to take the mail there. The situation may develop that he is obliged to stay there all night. He may decide after twelve o'clock that the ship in not coming and, instead of paying his board and lodging there, go back to his own community B.
That means that the next day, weather permitting, he must come back again and pick up the mail the ship has landed after the ship is in. Hence it is an expensive proposition because it means that the courier, who is a fisherman, must lose a day's fishing sometimes. It means that he may get stormbound while at the port of call and be obliged to pay board and lodging overnight. It means 67509-356
Post Office Act
all sorts of expenses that are not considered at all when these contracts are drawn up.
Then you have the third situation in which the mail is landed at a certain central port of call and you have a contractor who carries that mail around a circuit, calling at five or six different communities, probably travelling a distance of 40 or 50 miles. That is the most difficult situation of all because it involves all sorts of expenses, maintenance and vagaries of wind and weather which it is almost impossible to take into account at all, with the result that people who undertake these contracts soon find that they are losing money and they get out of them as quickly as they can.
I have had some cases in which we have not been able to get a postal service at all because we have not been able to find anybody who would carry the mail for what the post office considered a proper rate or a remunerative rate, considering the revenue which the service would yield.
As I said, some hon. members have expressed fear of patronage, but from my own experience I see very few opportunities for patronage in my province. The way the thing works there is that when a service is under contract, the regional supervisor or one of the local officials is the man who is obliged to search around and find out from the postmaster or some other people in the community who is willing to perform the service and for what price; and he is obliged to do a great deal of searching. When he has found somebody who is competent, with the necessary equipment such as a boat and so on- there is probably only one; there is probably nobody else interested-then he advises the authorities here in Ottawa who in turn advise the minister, and a contract is drawn up on that basis.
Very often the service is postponed and the contract is turned down because they cannot get a contractor to do the job for what the department is prepared to pay. In actual practice in my province I would say there is hardly any possibility of patronage. It is so difficult to get people to perform this service that if this amendment were carried, it would make the situation even worse and would cause hardship, particularly in my own riding.

At this time I fail to see any reasonableness in the minister's unwillingness to accept the amendment, which would merely ensure that at least once in the lifetime of every one of these office holders he would have to submit himself to a public competition, to bids. I see nothing wrong with that. I do not think anyone should be permitted to inherit a job. We do not have that in ordinary employment and I do not think we should have it in this type of employment either.
Some hon. members have mentioned the difficulties involved in getting any mail carriers at all in certain areas. There may well be areas of Canada where mail carriers are underpaid and others where they may be overpaid; and to have the occasional, at least a once in a lifetime, tender for each of these positions might serve a very useful purpose. It might bring those that are paid too much into line and in those areas where they are unable to get anyone to volunteer to take the position it might serve as a useful tool to convince the hierarchy in the Post Office Department that a higher rate of remuneration is necessary in that area. I fail to see any reasonable argument that the minister has put forth for his refusal to accept this amendment, unless he is willing to abolish the whole idea of calling for tenders, in which case the method now in vogue would have to disappear anyway.
The minister spoke of the difficulties in making temporary arrangements. That is no argument at all, because acceptance of the amendment would not add one single temporary arrangement to the deal. If there was no one willing to take over for the unexpired portion the minister would have to call for tenders in any event, and there would be no such thing as a temporary arrangement any more than is the case now. I feel very keenly that tenders should be called for, not necessarily at the beginning of a man's service but at least within a reasonable time; and I think it should be, as the amendment proposes, at the end of the contract period.

By way of conclusion rather than by way of introduction, it does seem to me that the minister has demonstrated clearly this afternoon that he will not accept any amendment to the bill before the committee that would cause tenders to be called for when letting these contracts. As I understand it, we have taken the position that in the event of inability for whatever reason of a man to carry on a rural mail contract, certain temporary problems are presented. We are in sympathy with those problems and we understand what those problems mean. We say to the minister that he can place that contract where he wishes for the duration of the contract, provided of course that it is not placed at a higher rate.
However, if it was proper that tenders should have been called for the original contract, then we submit that it is proper that tenders should be called when the contract passes to a new holder. We feel that the proper time for that is when the four years of the contract have run out and the contract comes up for consideration. speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 212, to amend the Telegraphs Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the present bill, as is said in the explanatory note, is to provide for the control of submarine cables terminating in or passing through

Canadian territory, excluding, however, submarine cables wholly under fresh water. My remarks, Mr. Speaker, will bear only on those that are affected by the bill, although I fully understand that in ordinary parlance the word "cable" would have a very extensive meaning.
I think it would facilitate the discussion of this measure if I were to set forth the pertinent facts so that the purposes the government has in mind may be clearly understood.
The part of the Telegraphs Act which deals with what the act calls "marine electric telegraph companies" and which prescribes the formalities to be followed by a company that desires to construct a telegraph wire or cable to connect any province with any other province of Canada or to extend beyond the limits of any province, was originally enacted in 1875. Section II of the original enactment- 38 Victoria, chapter 26-provided that until (a) the company had submitted to the governor in council a plan and survey of the proposed site and location of the cable and its approaches at the shore and of its stations, offices and accommodations on land and of all the intended works thereto appertaining; and until (b) such plan, site and location had been approved by the governor in council; and until (c) such conditions as he thought fit for the public good to impose touching the said telegraph and works had been complied with, the company might not exercise any of the powers conferred upon it by the act.
Though more than 75 years have elapsed since the Telegraphs Act was first enacted by parliament, there has been no substantial change in the language of the section to which I have just referred, and consequently no change in the formalities that must be observed by a company which wishes to lay and operate a submarine cable. I think hon. members will agree that it does not often happen that an enactment remains unchanged in substance for such a long time. The fact that there has been no change in the formalities to be followed is, I believe, explained by the way in which improvements in the general field of communications have developed.
When the act was passed originally in 1875 a submarine cable had a very limited capacity. In fact, it seems that at that time a cable usually carried two simplex circuits, each capable of transmitting about 26 words per minute. As the years passed improvements were made in the quality of cable construction and it was found possible gradually to increase the capacity of cables, but I should like to point out that the increase was not extraordinary if judged by present-day standards. In fact, the ultimate appeared to have been reached in 1923 with the installation of what is called a nonloaded cable

which, with the adding of repeaters, carried six circuits with a total speed of 252 words per minute. This is equal to 42 words per minute per circuit.
I think I should add that the older cables also were improved by various means so that their capacity with two circuits is now about 84 words per minute. Loaded cables were first introduced across the Atlantic in the mid-1920's and they made it possible to increase the number of circuits in the cable and also the total speed of the cable to as much as 500 words per minute. I mention these facts in order to point out that despite the improvements which have been developed the capacity of a cable was such that, of itself, it imposed an economic limitation on the number of cables that might be laid and consequently upon the number of additional circuits that might be established to compete with those which had been previously laid.
A further limitation upon the laying of new cables resulted from the development of wireless telegraphy or radio. As hon. members know, improvements in this field of radio have made it possible, in a relatively recent period, to use radio both for the transmission of telegraph signals and also for telephone conversations. In fact, since the expansion of this form of communication began in earnest only two new trans-Atlantic cables have been laid.
About 1950 a new technique was adopted to increase cable capacity and in that year the first submerged repeater to be placed in operation on a trans-Atlantic cable was installed at a distance of about 170 miles from Newfoundland in a cable laid in 1881. There is no unanimity apparently among technical men as to the extent to which repeaters will increase the speed of a cable. Some believe they will double the speed and others that they will treble it. No doubt the rate of increase depends upon a number of factors such as the nature of the cable, the distance from the shore, the kind of repeater, and so on.
I regret that it has seemed necessary to deal with these somewhat technical matters which, at first sight, seem perhaps not to be entirely relevant to the bill in order to stress one point in particular, and that is through improvements, installed in the cable itself or elsewhere, the capacity of most if not all of the trans-Atlantic cables has been increased over that which they originally had when the formalities prescribed by the Telegraphs Act were accomplished and when the requested approval of the governor in council was given. In stressing this point, I express no criticism of 67509-357J
Telegraphs Act
the action of any company in increasing the capacity of one or more of its cables, because the Telegraphs Act does not seem to prohibit it from doing so.
However, I must admit some concern that as the act now stands, once the requested permission to land the cable has been granted its capacity may be changed, perhaps quite substantially, without either the knowledge or consent of the government. Perhaps if the change in the capacity of a cable were to remain within the range I have indicated there might not be cause for great concern or for legislative action. However, the progress of science has gone much further and the development of coaxial cables with built-in repeaters, and their use for trans-oceanic communication, have completely changed the whole situation.
Hon. members will appreciate the significance of this development from the fact that the new trans-Atlantic telephone cable which is now being laid between Newfoundland and Scotland, and which is expected to come into operation later this year, will have a capacity equal to about 40 times the capacity of all existing trans-Atlantic cables. In this project two cables are being laid, one in each direction, and the transmission of each of these cables is at present expected to have a capacity of at least 800 telegraph circuits at 60 words per minute each. I say that the new cable is at present expected to have a capacity of 800 telegraph circuits, but the estimated total number has increased over the original figure and it is possible that at a later date it may be increased further.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that in speaking of the capacity of the trans-Atlantic telephone cable, and expessing it in terms of the number of circuits as I have just done, I want to make it clear that its primary purpose is for telephone and not for telegraphic purposes. I have merely used the number of telegraph circuits in order to emphasize the word-carrying capacity, so to speak, of these modern coaxial cables in relation to those that have already been laid and are now in operation. But I think the most important point to be stressed in that connection is that the introduction of the coaxial cable with the built-in repeaters has completely revolutionized the whole picture of trans-oceanic communications. I hope that hon. members have appreciated the fact that this trans-Atlantic telephone project, in effect, involves the laying of two cables that have 40 times the capacity of all the other cables that are already in existence. I think that in those circumstances hon. members will appreciate the necessity of amending the Telegraphs Act in order to meet the situation.

speechtext:
Thank you. I was just saying that at first sight it may appear as if the provisions of section 22 of the Telegraphs Act give the governor in council all the authority that is required, and that by the simple expedient of either granting or withholding approval on plans, site and location of the cable, the government may permit or may prevent the laying of new cables. In fact, however, the matter cannot be resolved in such a simple way; first, because the problem does not always arise in a way that admits of a yes or no solution; and, second, because under the present act there is no continuing control or regulation of the actions of a company with regard to the cable itself.
I should like to emphasize that if one reads section 22 of the Telegraphs Act, it will be found that what is contemplated seems to refer to actions that must be taken and completed before the cable comes into operation. In a word, they do not appear to be of the continuing character that would prevail and continue after the landing permit has been granted and the cable comes into operation. The problem, moreover, is complicated by the fact that most of the trans-Atlantic cables that are landed at some point in Canada serve primarily for the transmission of messages between the United States and the continent of Europe, or for what may be called through traffic.
The cables comprise two segments, one from Europe to Canada and the other from Canada to the United States, but they do serve also, although to a much lesser extent, for the transmission of messages originating in or destined for Canada. This is a complication because in a given case there might be no objection whatever to granting permission for a cable to carry through traffic, while there might be very real and valid objections to the provisions of facilities additional to those already established to meet Canadian requirements. Or alternatively, it

might appear desirable to limit the number of circuits to be opened in Canada. The present act does not appear to contemplate the attaching to the landing permit of conditions of a continuing nature and therefore does not seem to provide for revocation of the landing permit if the conditions are not observed.
The government believes that by establishing a licensing system it will be in a better position to deal more flexibly with applications for permission to land cables, to control the opening of circuits into Canada, and to regulate increases in the capacity of cables; and the amendment before the house has been drafted with these objects in mind.
There is one further point I wish to mention and that is the routing of messages originating in Canada. I am sure that hon. members share the feeling I have that it would be desirable if this business were routed to the cable heads in Canada over facilities located in Canada and owned and operated by Canadians. This would have the obvious effect of giving Canadians the maximum benefits to be derived from the business which they themselves originated.
Of course, I appreciate, just as I am sure hon. members do, that it would not always be possible for this to be achieved and that sometimes there would be reasons, such as the interruption of communications, overloading of facilities or other circumstance which might make it desirable in order to avoid delay that the traffic be carried over facilities in the United States; but in a general sense I think that Canadian traffic ought to move to the cable head by means of Canadian facilities. I feel sure the various companies operating cable facilities share this view and that so far as this is not now being done they will co-operate in helping us to achieve this objective; but I think I should point out that the proposed licensing system would enable us to exercise some measure of control over the routing of traffic originating in Canada.
I trust that with these explanations the bill will commend itself to the members of this house. May I add that if the bill receives second reading I shall then move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this bill is to go to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines there is no necessity to discuss it at any length at the present stage. I believe the minister is wise in referring it to that standing committee for several reasons. One is that there would appear to be some features about this activity which can be fully understood only after they have been explained by the experts and then I take it there may be some people who will be affected by this amendment who might wish to be heard before the committee and, of course, if the bill were dealt with in the house without being referred to the committee there would be no opportunity for such representations to be made.
We in the official opposition are curious about some aspects of this particular bill and while we are not opposing it at this stage we are reserving our right to do so in the event that the examination by the committee reveals the bill has features which in our opinion would justify opposition to it in the subsequent stages.
The minister opened his remarks today by pointing out that the Telegraphs Act has been in effect almost without amendment since 1875, a period of over 80 years. When he said that, it struck me as being rather strange that the bill having been so good originally and having been so good for over 80 years it should now be necessary to amend it and not by the usual type of amendment but merely by giving the government the power to license. In other words, here is another
Telegraphs Act
case in which we are establishing a licensing system to be fastened on the long suffering people of Canada. Apparently, judging from the minister's remarks, the main reason for taking this licensing power is to be able to limit the number of circuits. Evidently the government feels there are or may be too many cables and on that account there must be some power given to restrict them by licensing.
That would sound more reasonable if it were not for the fact the government itself is in the business in the shape of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, a crown company set up in 1949. It was set up at that time to take over external telecommunications but the minister of transport of that day on more than one occasion in the course of the discussion pointed out that it was not intended to give this crown company a monopoly. He may have been stretching his argument a bit but I find that at page 394 of Hansard for September 30, 1949, Mr. Chevrier had this to say:
It was asked whether the bill would create a monopoly. My reply is no, the bill will not create a monopoly.
And then he repeated that on the next page. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) had been referring to the possibility of the crown company being given a monopoly and Mr. Chevrier replied:
In any event, whether it is or is not the case, the Anglo-American Cable Company and Commercial Cable Company are in direct competition with both Cable and Wireless, Limited and Canadian Marconi Company, Limited,...
The latter two companies were taken over by Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation.
... so there is no danger of a monopoly. From what I understand, in the international field exclusive of the commonwealth field there are telecommunication services, both wireless and cable, that are quite strong and quite competitive in these services.
The minister was questioned further about that when the bill went before the committee in 1949, and at page 10 of the proceedings of the committee of November 8, 1949, we find this:
Some suggestion was made during the debate concerning monopoly. I will not go into that now because there are some technical officers here who will be able to do that. I do not think this nationalization will create a monopoly in any sense because there is a considerable amount of competition as it is now.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OP SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS

It will not, in so far as Canada is concerned.
We had that very definite statement by the minister in 1949. Even at that time there

Telegraphs Act
was some concern because there had been an agreement between various nations in the commonwealth with regard to telecommunications. In the very committee proceedings to which I have referred Mr. W. C. Connelly, superintendent of radio, Department of Transport, placed before the committee a memorandum relative to the subject under discussion. The memorandum points out that there had been an agreement reached between commonwealth countries for a reduction in the rates and that in that agreement the governments had agreed:
(a)	to maintain the policy of concentrating overseas telegraph traffic on the systems of Cable and Wireless Limited and its associates;
That was one of the companies taken over by the Canadian crown company.
(b)	to use their best endeavours to stop the circulation of traffic over foreign services using circuitous routes, and to resist the routing of traffic through foreign organizations not established in their respective territories where the Cable and Wireless Limited system has a suitable route which can carry the traffic;
I would point out the next two clauses.
(c)	to continue the policy of resisting the authorization or opening of new circuits which would be detrimental to Cable and Wireless Limited or its associates in the British empire;
(d)	to afford Cable and Wireless Limited and its associated companies overseas the opportunity of taking over on reasonable terms any external commercial wireless telegraph transmission services in the extra-European system at present operated by governments where or if such services compete with the companies' services;
That memorandum seems to be fairly clear as to the real objective in 1949 being to get a monopoly in external telecommunications services, and one wonders whether the amendment brought in today is not the next step to obtain that objective of a monopoly. There are other companies in the field which have been established for almost as long as the Telegraphs Act has been on the statute books of Canada and those companies are in a position to extend their services by way of additional circuits or to modernize their services. It may be that the real purpose of this bill is to force them out of business in Canada.
That brings up the question of whether the Canadian people are entitled to the benefits which would follow from fair competition, and I think that should receive the careful consideration of the standing committee. Any company operating under the Telegraphs Act is subject to drastic control, apart from the licensing control which the minister is now seeking to initiate. Such a company must obtain a charter from this parliament, and I believe they all have done so. Such a company must obtain a charter authorizing it to construct its cables.
IMr. Green.]
That control is set out in many sections of the act. The minister referred only to section 22. That section, in referring to any company coming under the Telegraphs Act, reads:
The company shall not exercise any of the powers by this part conferred until
(a)	the company has submitted to the governor In council, a plan and survey of the proposed site and location of such telegraph and its approaches at the shore, and of its stations, offices and accommodations on land and of all the intended works thereto appertaining,
(b)	such plan, site and location have been approved by the governor in council, and
(c)	such conditions as he thinks fit for the public good to impose touching the said telegraph and works, have been complied with.
That latter clause (c) gives the governor in council very wide powers. Section 24 provides:
(1)	Before commencing the construction of any such telegraph or work mentioned in section 23, or of any buoy or seamark connected therewith, the company shall deposit, at the Department of Transport, a plan thereof, for the approval of the minister.
(2)	In cases of emergency, for repairs to any work previously constructed or laid, the plan thereof shall be so deposited as speedily as may be after the commencement of the work.
Then section 25:
(1) The work shall not be constructed otherwise than in accordance with the plan as approved by the minister.
The section goes on to give the minister the power to remove the work if it has not been so constructed. Then section 26 provides for the use of lights and signals on ships used in connection with the work. Section 28 reads:
The minister may, at any time, at the expense of the company, cause to be made a survey and examination of any such work, buoy or sea-mark, or of the site thereof.
Section 29 gives the minister the right to recover any expense to which he is put by reason of checking the works of a company.
All these companies are also subject to control by the board of transport commissioners. As I read the act, the rates which they charge are subject to the approval of the board of transport commissioners. Section 31 reads:
(1) The company shall transmit all messages
(a)	in the order in which they are received or in such order as the board of transport commissioners for Canada may require or direct, and
(b)	at such rates as may be determined from time to time by the said board for the different classes of messages, or hours of the day or night during which such messages are transmitted, without discrimination within each class.
Section 32 provides:
The company may charge for the transmission of messages, and may demand and collect in advance such rates of payment therefor as are fixed by by-law of the company as its tariff rates and approved by the board of transport commissioners for Canada.

-giving the board of transport commissioners what appears to be full supervision of the activities of the company in the way of the charging of rates.
Now the minister proposes that there should in addition be a licensing control. He has given us no details of how that control is to be carried out. There is some suggestion that the crown company, Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, has a great deal to say in all these matters. Whilst, strictly speaking, the jurisdiction is given by statute to the Department of Transport, we hear rumours that the Department of Transport gets its advice from this crown company, which is certainly a competitor of the private companies.
We should be told in the committee whether the position is to be that the crown company is in effect to recommend the terms of the regulations and is to be the enforcing body. If that should come about, then we would have exactly the same position that has caused so much trouble in the radio field in Canada.
We should also be told in the committee whether this licensing control is to apply to existing companies already in the field or only to companies that enter it from now on. I take it from what the minister has said today that there is not much doubt that his intention is to cover all companies, no matter how long they have been in the business.
Does it also mean that all new outlets, all new circuits, are to be reserved to Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation? That would have the result in the long run of putting the other companies out of business and creating a government monopoly. I believe that there is no such cable landing licence law in the United Kingdom and also that, whilst there is a law of that nature in the United States, it is not as far-reaching as the one now proposed by the minister. These details, too, we shall require in the committee.
I submit that we cannot be too careful in making changes at this time. On the surface they seem to be innocuous, but where we have had a business established for so many years and carried on in a satisfactory manner there should not be drastic changes made without very good reason, and in this particular case the fact that there is this crown corporation, with its officers no doubt anxious for more power and out to build their own empire, I think, makes it all the more necessary that we should be cautious before agreeing to make changes of this kind.

I have been generally aware that some of the technological changes to which the minister referred in introducing this bill have been taking

place. Just how adequate the measure that the minister is now proposing will appear to us when we enter into that detailed discussion in the committee, of course, I do not feel I can say at this moment, but I feel I should indicate that, generally speaking, as far as I have been able to understand the bill, we are sympathetic to the purposes it is designed to achieve. The only qualms I have heard expressed about the bill, as a matter of fact, from the members of the group to which I belong in the house have come from my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron), who happens to have some of the poles that travel from the Banfield station crossing a piece of property he happens to own, and he is hoping that this bill will not interfere with the present rental arrangement he has with regard to those poles.

Nevertheless, I shall be looking forward with great interest to the study which this bill will receive in committee, as I know will those of my colleagues who also sit on that committee.

This is very important for us in Newfoundland. I was at the laying of the trans-Atlantic cable last year. It is a very expensive undertaking. It is something which has been badly needed between Europe and America, and I understand that when the laying of the cable is completed some 30 telephone communications will be handled simultaneously. The traffic in communications between Europe and America is growing all the time. I am very glad that the minister is sending the bill to the committee so that these cable companies which have operated in Newfoundland for many years can make their representations to the committee and, if necessary, safeguard any of the rights they already possess. Mr. Speaker, I am not going to attempt to deal with all the remarks that have been made but I should like to say one or two words before the debate concludes. In my remarks on the bill and in dealing with the history, so to speak, of the cables that now exist, and referring particularly to the trans-Atlantic telephone cable which is now in process of being laid, I particularly wished to stress the fact that technological developments, if I may call them by that name, have completely changed the picture from the time when the Telegraphs Act was adopted, when the word-carrying capacity of a cable was

distinctly limited, to the present time when we have cables of the nature of the transAtlantic telephone cable, a coaxial cable incorporating in it repeaters at intervals of approximately 40 miles apart, which has expressed in terms of telegraph circuits, as many as 800 circuits capable of carrying 60 words per minute each.
I cannot help thinking that this technological development makes it necessary for us to introduce legislation of the kind that is embodied in the bill now before the house. May I say to those who seemed to think that in the bill is the means of establishing a monopoly in favour of Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation that it would not be necessary to adopt this legislation if the government had any such purpose in mind because, as I thought I made clear in my earlier remarks, by the simple process of saying no to all applications in the future to land cables it would follow that there could be no other cables added to those that now exist. Therefore if that had been the purpose it would not have been necessary to introduce this legislation in order to create the monopoly, to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) referred. There is no intention, just as I may say there was no intention in 1949, of creating a monopoly in favour of C.O.T.C.
I had the occasion quite recently to read the debate at that time and to go over the evidence that was given by my predecessor. I do not think anything has happened in the meantime which would in any way invalidate the statements he made at that time.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra expressed the fear that C.O.T.C. would be the regulatory body. I may say at once that no such thought has ever crossed the minds of those who have drafted the legislation or the officials of my own department. I should like to correct any impression that may exist that C.O.T.C. was our sole adviser in the matter of telecommunications. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra well knows, there is a telecommunications division in the Department of Transport staffed with most competent officials, and when we need advice on matters in this particular field quite frankly it is not necessary for us to go outside the department itself. Consequently I can set at rest the doubts he may have in mind that C.O.T.C. would be the regulatory body either to enact or to administer the regulations which it is contemplated will be made if this legislation is adopted.
The next point was whether this legislation applies to existing companies. The answer to that question, of course, is that
Income Tax Act
it is intended to apply to all companies operating cables, and it is not intended that it would merely apply to the operation of cables that might hereafter be laid.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) also referred to legislation in the United Kingdom. My information on that subject is that in the United Kingdom, under the Telegraphs Act, the Postmaster General is empowered to grant written licences on such pecuniary or other terms as he may deem proper, either generally or in any individual case to any company, person or body to transmit telegrams. My understanding is that at the present time there are no licences in force for the cables from Canada to the United Kingdom and that they are, if you like, so to speak on the sufferance of the Postmaster General. That is not the situation in Canada. I am not suggesting that the situation should be that all other cables should cease to exist. Far from it. If we wanted to create a monopoly, as my hon. friend fears, we certainly would not have proceeded to do it in this way.
Mr. Speaker, I fully realize that this is a technical measure and that there are many associated questions of a technical nature. It was my thought, in referring it to the committee, that hon. members would have an opportunity of obtaining such additional information as they needed in order to come to the conclusion, I hope, that the legislation is sound and that it deals with a situation that has developed since the advent of the coaxial cable.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
