speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 418, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has moved the second reading of Bill No. 418, to amend the Income Tax Act. This cannot be a repetition of the budget debate nor, as the Speaker said on June 29, 1955, can the debate on second reading of the income tax amending bill be in itself a miniature budget debate. Had the rule been otherwise, there are many

Income Tax Act
things that one would have wished to discuss at this time including questions as to the credit restrictions and other matters of a financial or fiscal nature which are calling for attention on the part of the house at this present time.
It is not always easy, Mr. Speaker, to define the principle of the annual income tax amending bill. It is an annual bill and, in this respect, it presents an annual problem. In fact, the income tax amending bill is almost always just a collection of individual amendments, some related to each other and some quite heterogeneous. I suppose as close as we can come to the principle of such a bill, Mr. Speaker, would be to say this, that the Income Tax Act should be reviewed and amended with a view to correcting injustices, weaknesses and oppressive effects.
It is desirable that there should be a periodical parliamentary review not only of what the government may consider each year to be necessary amendments to the Income Tax Act but of the Income Tax Act as a whole. When this act was first brought before the house to succeed the old Income War Tax Act, it will be remembered that the bill was referred to the banking and commerce committee and that that committee undertook a review of that legislation. That review was perhaps not as extensive as some would have wished it to be, but at any rate the matter came before one of the select committees of the house.
There are many people who consider that, when they submit proposals to the Minister of Finance or the government's financial authorities in relation to needed amendments to the act, those matters automatically come before the house. Hon. members, of course, well know that they do not necessarily come before the house at all. They do not come before the house unless the government chooses to bring them before the house in the income tax amending bill. I do not intend to repeat at length what I said on this subject last year as reported at page 5436 of Hansard of June 29, but I think that from time to time public hearings ought to be conducted by a select committee of the house-and I think the banking and commerce committee is eminently suited for that purpose-at which time the committee could review the entire act and receive representations by interested bodies which have a case to make with regard to any features of the act, any shortcomings in it or the administration of the act.
My next comment relates to the language in which our income tax legislation is couched. To an ever-increasing degree our income tax legislation becomes more complicated. The problem of interpretation of our

tax legislation is becoming ever increasingly intensified. The act abounds in abstruse provisions, complicated sections, subsections, clauses, subclauses and provisos. It is written in terms that challenge the intelligence and understanding of specialists both of the legal and the accounting professions, and in many cases the co-operation of both is required in the interpretation of the provisions of the act. It is an unhappy paradox that the Income Tax Act, which most directly affects most people, is written in terms most difficult for them to understand. It may not be possible to go as far as one would wish to go in couching legislation on this subject in simple terms, but at any rate a serious effort ought to be made to do so.
This year, Mr. Speaker, the resolution preceding the introduction of the bill was perhaps the briefest that we have had. Certainly only three short resolutions were put before the committee of ways and means. The only three subjects which touched on the balance of ways and means and therefore found their way into the resolutions were proposals in relation to employees' profit-sharing plans, deduction of expenses of persons attending conventions, and depletion allowances. Those are all the matters of which the house was given advance information in the resolutions. Hence this year we approach a bill on which little information has been given at the preceding resolution stage.
I wish to submit to the house, Mr. Speaker, that our income taxes are too high. The minister has proposed no reductions in income tax this year. In the fiscal year which ended March 31, 1956 the government collected in personal income taxes $1,180 million.
In the fiscal year which commenced April 1, 1956, the minister has forecast that he will collect $1,265 million in personal income taxes. Similarly, under this same measure, the minister announced that collection last year from the corporation tax amounted to $1,035 million and forecast he would collect from the corporation tax this year $1,315 million.
Thus, it will be seen, Mr. Speaker, that out of expected revenues of $4,763 million in the present fiscal year, including $360 million of non-tax revenues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) expects to collect 26-5 per cent of his total revenue by means of personal income taxes and 28 per cent by means of the tax on corporations. In other words, sir, we are here dealing with a statute, the Income Tax Act, under which the minister this year proposes to collect 54-5 per cent of his total expected revenues, including those from nontax sources.

This leads me to make a comment, sir, on what we now know of the fiscal results of the first two months of the present fiscal year. We have the figures already for the months of April and May. The minister, in his budget speech, indicated that he is basing his budget forecast on a gross national product of "about $28 billion". We now know that in the first quarter of 1956 the gross national product was running at the rate of $28-3 billion or perhaps a little more than the minister took into account at the time he made his budget forecast. The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of June 21, 1956, contains this paragraph:
The rise in Canada's gross national product which has been going on for a year-and-a-half continued into the first quarter of 1956, with the increase in the value of production from the fourth quarter amounting to close to 3 per cent after allowing for seasonal factors. This recent increase has raised the level of gross national product to an annual rate of $28 -3 billion or about 6 per cent above the annual average for the year 1955 as a whole, and 11-7 per cent above the first quarter one year ago. The continued advance in the first three months of this year was mainly a reflection of a further rise in the physical volume of production, with prices on average showing only a small increase.
It is quite evident, Mr. Speaker, that if taxes continue at the present rate and if the gross national product is thus to increase, unless the spending machine is just to be turned loose, a very big surplus for the present fiscal year is now assured.
Look at the results of the first two months of the present fiscal year. In the months of April and May, 1956, revenues amounted to $780,500,000 and expenditures to $506,300,000, so that in those two months the minister had a surplus of $274,200,000. Now, we have been told often that you must not count surpluses before the end of the fiscal year, and that is quite true. We are aware as well that there are certain expenditures that bulk larger in the closing months of the fiscal year than they do in the earlier months. But surely it is a fair test to apply the results of the first two months of the fiscal year to those of the previous year.
In those two corresponding months of 1955, namely, April and May, the revenues that were collected in the treasury were $611,300,000 and expenditures were $474,700,000. The surplus for those two months was accordingly $136,600,000. You will see, then, that while expenditures advanced this year in the two months from $474,700,000 to $506,300,000, revenues showed a very much larger increase from $611,300,000 to $780,500,000. The surplus for the two months increased from $136,600,000 in 1955 to $274,200,000 this year. The surplus thus practically doubled for the two
Income Tax Act
months. It is quite evident that given a continuation of the present high rates of taxation, a continuation of the present high gross national product without any deliberate turning loose of the government's spending machine, a very large surplus is assured for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that in view of these unchallengeable facts a reduction in the rate of income tax ought to be made now and ought to be made under the present measure. The government, in my submission, has no business, has no right, to go on exacting this very high rate of taxation when the end result is going to be a huge surplus of revenues over expenditures.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I had reached the point just prior to the dinner adjournment where I had submitted to the house that there ought to be a reduction in the income tax at this time. The failure of the present bill to make any provision for a reduction in the income tax must be measured against a background which is pressing on the attention of thinking Canadians these days with increasing seriousness.
Canada is suffering today from a lack of risk capital. In the first three months of 1956 Canada suffered a substantial current deficit which has been described in the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of June 15 as follows:
Canada's current deficit from transactions in goods and services with other countries rose to a new peak for the first quarter of $345 million. This compares with $174 million in the first quarter last year and $255 million in the fourth quarter. This is about the same size as the highest quarterly deficit yet to appear which occurred in the second quarter of 1951. In relative terms too, the deficit is much higher than last year when it averaged almost 12 per cent of current receipts. At 25 per cent of current receipts it now represents almost the same proportion of current receipts as in 1930.
The new factor contributing to the large deficit was the massive size of the import balance on commodity account which amounted to $190 million. The deficit from all other current transactions of $155 million was slightly less than in the corresponding quarter last year. Until recently the principal elements in the current deficit in the past few years have originated in these "invisible" transactions in the absence of surpluses on commodity account. But since the fourth quarter of 1955 the appearance of a large import balance on commodity account has contributed greatly to the over-all current deficit and in this year it has been the major element for the first time since early in 1951.

Income Tax Act
That commodity trade deficit, Mr. Speaker, has reached very alarming proportions. In the entire year 1955, Canada had an over-all trade deficit on commodity account of $360 million, and in our trade with the United States alone Canada sustained a trading deficit of $840 million. In the first quarter of 1956, on commodity trading account, Canada sustained an over-all deficit of $190 million and in our commodity trade with the United States a deficit of $400 million. That was in the first quarter of this year; our deficit on commodity trading account with the United States was half what it was in the entire year of 1955 when this tremendous deficit of $840 million was incurred in our commodity trading account with the United States.
How is this deficit being paid? How is it being financed? It is being financed, Mr. Speaker, by borrowing capital from abroad and in effect as a nation we are going into debt by importing capital in order to pay for a current deficit in our trade. We are buying so much more from the United States than we are selling to her that we are paying for the difference, we are meeting the deficit, by borrowing in the form of imported capital.
As many distinguished and thoughtful Canadians are pointing out today, the most pressing need in our whole national program of investment so far as the source of capital for that program is concerned is of more Canadian capital for that purpose. Some leading Canadians have stressed this in recent days. For instance, at the conference of the investment dealers' association of Canada held last month at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, this note was sounded by several leaders in the industrial life of this country. Mr. Thomas W. Eadie, the president of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, speaking of the tremendous need of capital for expansion in the next 25 years, said:
I see no reason why the major part of this vast sum should not be obtained from Canadian sources.
Mr. W. J. Bennett, the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, speaking of the need for capital to finance development in the future, said:
I hope that a substantial part of this financing will be supplied by Canadian investment houses.
The report in summary concludes:
All speakers during the two days of business sessions predicted a big year ahead for Canada, a busy time for the investment business, and stressed the need for Canadians to invest in their country's growth.
Sir, where is the capital coming from Canadian sources to invest in this country's growth? There is only one source and that is

in savings; the savings of the people or the profits of enterprise, either corporate or personal.
The amount of capital that is going to be available in these forms depends on how much is left in the hands of those who earn after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has taken his tax cut out of those earnings. If we refer to the recent publication of the dominion bureau of statistics, national accounts, income and expenditure for the first quarter of 1956, we see on page 13 some interesting figures with regard to total personal savings.
In the year 1953 the total personal savings in Canada amounted to $1,588 million. In
1954	that figure had dropped substantially to $965 million. In the year 1955 it had risen somewhat to $1,312 million. In the first quarter of 1956 it was just $209 million. Now, that happens to be a little more than in the first quarter of 1955 but it is substantially less than the quarterly average for
1955	and correspondingly less than the quarterly average in some of those preceding years to which I have referred. Therefore, I say, Mr. Speaker, the need of creating Canadian capital, having regard to the needs of developing the resources of this country, is more pressing than ever before. If Canadian capital is to take a fair share and part in the development of the resources of this country it can come about only through the means of savings and they depend entirely on how much the Minister of Finance is going to leave of the earnings of people of this country after he has taken his tax cut.
Canadians have a high standard of living; they spend quite freely. Then where will they save? There is no relief in this bill from the present too high rate of income tax in this country. It is inevitable that we shall continue to lack Canadian capital as long as we have in this country the present crushing burden of income taxation. A reduction in the rate of income tax is very badly needed at the present time but none has been forthcoming and apparently Canadians for this purpose must await the election exigencies of the government.
I would like to conclude what I said on second reading of the bill, sir, by pointing to ten matters which should have been dealt with in the income tax amending bill this year but which have escaped attention on the part of the government.
The first, of course, is the fact that there are no tax reductions; I have already dealt with that.
The second is that no provision has been made for increases in the exemptions. These

exemptions of $2,000 for married persons and $1,000 for single persons have been in effect now for a very long time. Similarly, the exemptions of $150 for a dependent child under 16 years of age and $400 for a dependent child of greater age have been in effect for a very long time now. Those exemptions go back to the days when the Canadian dollar had some real value but they do not fit the situation today, and the Minister of Finance might well address his efforts and his thinking to the necessity for granting reductions in taxation by taking that first step of proposing to the house an increase in the present exemptions. We were reminded by a very distinguished Canadian tax authority just a fortnight ago that the man who was earning $5,000 before the war must make $10,480 today or his financial position has deteriorated. That was the statement of Mr. J. Harvey Perry, director of the Canadian Tax Foundation to a joint convention of the General Accountants Association of Canada and the Certified General Accountants Association of Ontario on June 16. He added:
Most people are working as hard as they can but it doesn't seem reasonable that 30 per cent or 40 per cent of every dollar they earn goes to government-it's discouraging.
So I submit that the minister should have proposed an increase in these exemptions.
Third, this bill proposes no definition of capital gains. I do not intend to go into this or other subjects at length, but I do wish to mention this subject. It has already had some discussion at an earlier stage in the present session. I simply wish to assert that very definitely a definition of capital gains is urgently needed in the Income Tax Act. It is a striking fact that our Income Tax Act contains no definition of "income" and similarly it contains no definition of what are capital gains. The income tax appeal board and the courts are now dealing with some very difficult cases in regard to what constitutes a capital gain as distinguished from income. The old judicial definitions are no longer adequate to protect from taxation under this statute gains which are of the nature of capital and should not be classified under modern conditions as income. I simply leave this subject with the quotation of the final sentence of a very brilliant discourse by Mr. H. Heward Stikeman, Q.C., on a recent occasion when speaking on the subject "The Vanishing Capital Gain". After indicating the number of rules that anyone must now observe if he hopes to preserve the capital nature of a gain, concluded:
Only by some legislative act can the uncertainty which now exists be removed.
The minister had a golden opportunity this year to bring in an amendment to give an
Income Tax Act
adequate definition to capital gains but he has taken no step in that regard.
Fourth, the minister has not proposed any increase in the present $20,000 limit set by section 39 of the Income Tax Act as the figure up to which corporate income is taxed at the lower 20 per cent rate instead of the 47 per cent rate. This figure of $20,000 as the maximum of corporate income for this purpose was set some years ago and it is high time, having regard to modern conditions and the depreciation of the dollar in the interval, that the maximum was substantially increased.
The fifth matter is the subject of contributions for pension purposes by recognized groups of self-employed. This is not a new subject, as it has been discussed regularly at each of the last three sessions to my personal knowledge, but again the minister has not devoted a syllable to the subject in either his resolutions or his budget speech. Here is a problem urgently crying for redress. Under section 11 of the act it is permissible for employer and employees to provide for approved pension plans and to deduct their contributions to such plans from their taxable income. But in the case of the self-employed members of professional and other groups, there is no provision in our law today even where the group is clearly defined to enable them to enjoy similar benefits under the Income Tax Act.
This has been the subject of effective representations to the minister or his predecessor by a number of leading national professional and other groups such as the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Dental Association, the national labour bodies of this country, the Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada, and many others, in concert. It is to be noted that remedial steps in this regard have been taken in the United Kingdom where an intensive study was applied by a royal commission to the problem, but here in Canada we continue to await some action on the part of the government. I am renewing the pleas which I made, and which others have made on previous occasions, that the government propose amendments to the act which will make it possible for well-defined groups of self-employed persons to enjoy the benefits now extended to employers and employees under the act in relation to contributions to pension schemes.
The sixth matter is the position of the tax-exempt spouse. I mention this briefly as I spoke on it previously on June 29, 1955, as reported on page 5436 of Hansard of that day. This matter was the subject of representations

Income Tax Act
made to the minister by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in February, 1955, and the following was their proposal:
When the income of a wife is over $250 but below $1,000, the excess of her income is in effect added to the income of her husband through a reduction of his marital exemption. If the income of the wife is composed of dividends, the 20 per cent tax credit is lost. Accordingly, it is recommended by the executive council that in such cases the husband be allowed the 20 per cent tax credit on that portion of the dividends received by his wife on which he has to pay tax.
I submit that that is a sound recommendation, but it has received no recognition from the minister in the two budgets he has brought into this house since those representations were made to him. I say that the present measure is lacking in that it continues to ignore this problem.
The seventh problem relates to alimony or maintenance payments, and here a glaring injustice and inequality exists, one that has claimed the attention of the income tax appeal board as well as groups associated with social problems. Section 11 (1) (1) of the act permits the deduction by a taxpayer of an amount paid in these terms:
(1) an amount paid by the taxpayer in the year pursuant to a decree, order or judgment of a competent tribunal in an action or proceeding for divorce or judicial separation or pursuant to a written separation agreement as alimony or other allowance payable on a periodic basis for the maintenance of the recipient thereof, children of the marriage, or both the recipient and children of the marriage, if he is living apart from the spouse or former spouse to whom he is required to make the payment.
The inadequacy of that definition has become more apparent during the past year than ever before. I am sure it has been brought to the attention of the minister and yet nothing has been done in the present bill to cope with it.
In the province of Ontario-I am sure the situation obtains in other provinces as well- if a payment is made by a husband toward the support of a wife, under a judgment of the Supreme Court of Ontario in an action or proceeding for divorce, then the amount may be deducted by the husband from his taxable income. But, if the money is being paid pursuant to an order made in the family court by a judge of that court acting with magisterial power under the Deserted Wives and Children's Maintenance Act, the payment that he so makes is not deductible by him from taxable income. Having regard to the fact that there are so many orders made in these cases in the family courts, you have some appreciation, Mr. Speaker, of the extent of the problem and the injustice that is created in such a multiplicity of cases.

That is one aspect of the problem. There is another. Last October a case came before the income tax appeal board and was adjudicated upon there by Mr. Commissioner Fordham. In a judgment that he handed down on October 12, 1955, he is quoted in the press as pointing out that the law now allows deduction of alimony payments only where there is a judicial separation or divorce; otherwise, alimony is not deductible, and in Ontario there is no such thing as judicial separation. His judgment proceeded to draw attention to the weaknesses of the present act and the injustices created by the definition that I have quoted.
For my part, I had assumed that, when that matter came to the public attention in such a direct way in the judgment of Mr. Commissioner Fordham, the Department of Finance would have taken note of the problem and we should have had before us now some new definition of alimony so that the injustice now so apparent might be remedied; but the present bill is silent on this subject as well.
He said that it was an obvious oversight in the drafting of the act.

My hon. friend from Hamilton West reminds me that Mr. Commissioner Fordham referred to this matter as an obvious oversight in the drafting of the law. These were his words:
This matter reveals for the first time, where the board is concerned, what appears to be a remarkable and unfortunate oversight in the drafting of (the law).
Although alimony, as such, is clearly deductible by the payer when a court has made an award of alimony in a decree, order or judgment for divorce, or a husband and wife have executed a separation agreement providing for the payment of alimony, . . . (the law) does not take cognizance of an action for alimony alone.
The matter is one that would appear to merit early consideration by parliament, as the fact that the appellant's wife sued for alimony alone and not for a divorce as well, presents an extraordinary ground for having to refuse the husband the right to deduct the amounts of any alimony payments from his taxable income.
This is a palpable and manifest injustice, and only parliament can correct it. It is not something that occurred to the members of this house when that definition was first introduced into the Income Tax Act. It surprised me not a little, in the face of that clear exposition of the problem by Mr. Commissioner Fordham as long ago as last October, that the subject has not been deemed by the Minister of Finance worthy of redress.
The eighth matter in which this bill is lamentably lacking is the want of clarification of foreign exchange transactions. This matter has been before the department actively

within the past year, and yet the subject is ignored in the present bill.
The ninth matter I should like to mention briefly is the subject of the so-called "nil" assessments. It is an extraordinary fact that, in the cases where the notice of assessment is issued showing the word "nil" in defining the amount remaining to be paid, it has been held that that is not an assessment at all. I am sure that must shock the sensibilities of most people. When they receive their notice of assessment-and most of them, I have no doubt, come in this form-and the word "nil" simply appears under the heading "balance payable", most people would certainly conclude that that was an assessment. It appears on a notice of assessment; but the courts have ruled on various occasions that that so-called "nil" assessment is no assessment at all, and therefore any correcting assessment at a later date becomes the original assessment.
This situation has left many persons and many business enterprises up in the air, in a condition of uncertainty as to their tax position, and it is creating much difficulty and suspense. Surely this is something that calls for redress, and yet it likewise has escaped attention on the part of the minister in the present bill. This has important results, of course, as all hon. members will appreciate, in determining the date under various provisions of the Income Tax Act from which time runs. I think it shocks the sensibilities of most members to find that a nil assessment is no assessment at all. That is something that calls for redress. In view of the finding of the courts, redress must come from parliament; yet the government offers parliament no opportunity in that regard this year.
The tenth and final matter that I should like to mention relates to an injustice that exists under section 116 (4) of the act and has been drawn to the attention of the government already on behalf of the Canadian Bar Association. Let me interject here that in selecting these ten subjects I am not suggesting for one minute that they exhaust the shortcomings in the present measure or the list of subjects urgently calling for redress in our income tax legislation; but, time being short and some of these other subjects having been touched on before, I shall not go beyond this last of my group of ten. Section 116 (4) provides:
The minister may, if he considers it advisable in a particular case, accept security for payment of taxes by way of mortgage or other charge of any kind whatsoever on property of the taxpayer or any other person or by way of guarantee from other persons.
Here is an actual situation that has arisen. A mortgage was taken by the minister and
Income Tax Act
registered as a second mortgage. There was already a valid first mortgage registered against the property of the taxpayer. The first mortgage having fallen into arrears, the first mortgagee sought to enforce his security. He sought to take foreclosure proceedings but he found that, while he could foreclose the owner of the equity of redemption, he had no power to take action to bring about a foreclosure of the second mortgage held by the minister. It may possibly be that he will have the right to sell under his power of sale, and in that way wipe out the second mortgage held by the minister. That may be a debatable point; I am not expressing any opinion on that subject at the moment; but the fact is that, if the first mortgagee in that case wishes to take the normal proceeding of foreclosure, he has no way at all of bringing about foreclosure on that second mortgage held by the minister. That is something that calls for redress. It is not fair, and that subject, although known to the minister and his department, has escaped all attention in the present bill.
So, Mr. Speaker, while the bill may look long in terms of bulk, and while many of its provisions are remedial in form and intent and will certainly have support on that basis, nevertheless there are many shortcomings in the bill. There are many injustices in our income tax legislation crying for redress which it lay within the power of the minister to propose in this measure but which have escaped the attention of the minister and of the department. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the day is not far removed when some minister of finance will have the courage to grapple with these problems and bring forward legislative proposals for the redress of them.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I have very little in common with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). He said a number of things which I cannot accept. He complains about the income tax in Canada being too high. He says that Canadians have a high standard of living. I think it is a mistake to make general statements of that sort. Some Canadians have a very high standard of living. A great many Canadians have a standard that is not high enough.

I think the hon. member will agree that I was speaking about national standards in relation to national needs of capital and national needs of saving, and it was a matter of comparing them with other countries.

I think the suggestion of the hon. member that we should be giving relief to the people who are fortunate

Income Tax Act
enough to be paying income tax is not the type of suggestion that should be made seriously at this particular time. It is true that the over-all Canadian economy is very buoyant. The hon. member for Eglinton referred to the last national accounts which have come to us, and while he was concerned about the slight drop in savings I think he might have mentioned that personal disposable income is up over 10 per cent for the first quarter of 1956 compared with the same period a year ago.
At the supper hour I received in the mail the Carrot River Observer. There is a publisher's note intimating that although he has been a newspaper publisher for 13 years and has been in Carrot River for eight years the last issue of the Observer will come out about the middle of July. The editor is leaving for the city to take a secretarial course for the next ten months. This points up the crisis that confronts agriculture. The people who have been supporting this newspaper derive their livelihood from agriculture, and there is no future for a newspaper in a farming community if the farmers are in the position that farmers all across Canada now find themselves. That should be a matter of some concern to us.
I should like to draw the attention of the house and particularly that of the member for Eglinton to the recent bureau of statistics paper on the distribution of non-farm income in Canada for 1954. A year ago I used a similar paper that dealt with income for the year 1951 and at that time a number of hon. members said: "Oh yes, but the position now is a good deal brighter than it was in 1951." What is the position in 1954? For the purposes of this study the family is defined as follows:
. . . a group of individuals sharing a common dwelling unit and related by blood, marriage or adoption. Thus, all relatives living together were considered to comprise one family unit whatever the degree of family relationship . . .
Then there is the following with respect to the definition of an individual:
"Individuals" in tables 14 to 23 are defined as all persons aged 14 and over receiving income in 1954 and whose major source of income was from sources other than farming or military pay.
This leaves out of consideration the 20 per cent of the Canadian people who are engaged in agriculture and who are in a depressed condition as has been pointed out before. But here we have the non-farm people. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) does not consider that a single person earning under $1,000 a year should have to pay income tax. I think it would be a logical conclusion that for a single person $1,000 is the minimum that a citizen should have
if he or she is going to be able to get a fair share of Canadian income. But what percentage of Canadian individuals are getting less than $1,000 a year? We have a breakdown here according to regions. In the Atlantic provinces 54 per cent of individuals are getting less than $1,000. In Quebec the position is better in that there are 38.4 per cent who are getting less than $1,000. In Ontario the figure is 36.7 per cent, in the prairie provinces 42.2 per cent and in British Columbia 49.5 per cent.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that with percentages of individuals getting less than $1,000 a year ranging from 36 per cent in Ontario to 54 per cent in the Atlantic provinces we should be worrying about this large sector of the Canadian economy rather than the fortunate Canadian citizens who are able to pay income tax. Let us look at the next group, the families, and I am going to refer to the percentages of families in Canada who are receiving less than $2,000 a year. In the Atlantic provinces 39-8 per cent are receiving less than $2,000 a year. In Quebec the figure is 16-6 per cent, in Ontario 9-8 per cent, in the prairie provinces 17-1 per cent and in British Columbia 17 per cent.
In a country as prosperous as Canada I am sure this is a matter of real concern to the Minister of Finance who should be regarded as the individual who is trying to see that the fiscal policy adopted is such that the 15 million people who live in Canada may have a fair share of the wealth produced by the activity of all our people and that the people in the different regions should, as a result of the fiscal policy, be able to do something about their general position.
In addition to the figures I have given regarding the position of Canadians generally, which I am sure is a very different position from that which the member for Eglinton has in mind, I should like to refer to the Bank of Canada statistical summary for April of this year and in particular to the report on consumer credit outstanding. At the end of the last quarter of 1951 charge accounts in stores stood at $283 million, and at the end of the last quarter of 1955 they were $376 million. Then we come to instalment accounts with retail dealers. For 1951 the figure was $123 million and by the end of the last quarter of 1955 it was up to $377 million. For finance companies this amount has jumped from $186 million to $610 million. Totalling all these, for charge accounts, retail dealers and finance companies the amount has increased from $309 million to $987 million. Those of us who remember the disastrous depression that occurred in the thirties and the crash that occurred in the late twenties should remem-

ber that one of the warning signals that was so obvious then was the disturbing increase in credit buying and the percentage of the expendable income that had to go to pay interest on debts which were mounting. The total for these selected items is shown as being $973 million at the end of December, 1951. That figure at the end of 1955 stood at $2,193 million. I therefore submit, Mr. Speaker, that with this large group of Canadian people who are not getting enough to pay income tax, the minister should not be unduly concerned about the fact that some Canadians are worrying about their corporation profits. The last report on corporation profits that I received from the bureau deals with the last quarter of 1955. It says this:
Corporation profits after taxes in the fourth quarter of 1955 rose an estimated $153 million or 53 per cent from $291 million in 1954 to $444 million in 1955. Cumulative profits after taxes for the 12 months of 1955 increased an estimated $426 million, or 35 per cent, over the corresponding period of the previous year, from $1,230 million in 1954 to $1,656 million in 1955.
The last taxation statistics supplied by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) give us some interesting tables with regard to Canadians who pay income tax. I wish hon. members would keep in mind these figures which I gave and which show that in the maritime provinces 54 per cent of the individuals received less than $1,000. When it comes to those who pay income tax there is an interesting table showing the breakdown according to occupations. Medical doctors head the list with an average income of $11,200. Consulting engineers come next with $10,200. Lawyers and notaries are down a little bit with $9,900; accountants, $8,000; dentists, $7,400 and so on down the list. At the bottom of the list come nurses with $1,800. If you average out the incomes that are given by those who pay income taxes, you will find an average of $3,143. There is another breakdown giving the percentage of our people in these various categories.
Before the minister hastens to give relief to those who are paying income tax, I think it is imperative that he evolve a fiscal policy so that, some way or other the large number of Canadians who have never paid income tax may be placed in a position where they have ways of spending money so that we do not have in the maritimes, for example, 33 per cent of individuals under $500 and in Quebec 22 per cent under $500. The minister must do something about the situation where 90 farmers out of 100 in Canada do not receive a taxable income. I submit that he has machinery available so that assistance can be given.
I hope he will not take too seriously the 10 suggestions made by the hon. member for
Income Tax Act
Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). I was not able to estimate what reduction in the federal revenue would result if these proposals were acted upon. I am not going to make any suggestions to the minister as to where he should cut down. At one point the hon. member for Eglinton complained about the amount of money the people of Canada are paying in taxes. In view of the fact that the official opposition makes that criticism so often and never suggests a five-cent piece that could be saved in connection with the discussion of any particular estimate, I think it is not too constructive to suggest that the people of Canada are complaining about the taxes they are paying. I think the people of Canada want to be satisfied that the taxes they are paying are being spent wisely. I think they want to be satisfied that the old people and the young will get more favourable consideration than they are now receiving. I am not even going to press for the proposal that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has made so frequently, namely that the 3 per cent floor relationship to the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes should be included. This matter has been discussed and while the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made a very good case, it has been turned down. I am not going to press for this small percentage of Canadian people having relief in this particular connection.
I find that a year ago, when this matter was before us, I made some study of the position of the people who are paying large amounts in corporation taxes and personal income taxes. I find that the taxpayer who has an income of $100,000 a year is really asked to make a substantial payment to the income tax authorities. But I think most people will agree that if you are in that fortunate position where you have a taxable income of $100,000, you would not worry so much about how much you had to pay so long as you had a sizeable amount left. It appears to me that with $163 per day for 300 days in the year left for yourself, you should not complain too much. I find that a taxpayer who has an income of $200,000 a year, although he pays a large amount in dollars, has left $261 a day. I find that a taxpayer in a higher bracket still, one with $400,000 a year income, has left $419.38 per day. I therefore submit that, in planning for the future, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) should keep in mind the fact that no nation can long survive with one group of people as prosperous as are one section of the Canadian people while such a large number of the Canadian people have not been able to get in a position-as single people or as

Income Tax Act
married individuals-where they are able to pay income tax of any sizeable amount.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take much time on the bill that is before us, but I think there are some things that ought to be said at this stage in the hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) will give them his earnest consideration and that perhaps, by the time we get to the discussion of the bill in committee, he will be prepared to give consideration to one or two proposals that I intend to make. I am glad to have the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) here to hear what I have to say on one feature of the bill because he is charged with the responsibility of administering the Income Tax Act while the minister is charged with the responsibility of dealing with financial policy as reflected in it. Now, I do not wish in anything I say to cast a reflection on either minister, but I am going to be somewhat critical of the attitude of some of the people who do administer the act. I am going to speak now in general terms.
This Bill No. 418, as I see it, is divided into two main parts. As I look at them, there are the general provisions that are there for the purpose of giving relief, if we wish to put it that way, to certain groups of taxpayers in this country, or perhaps it would be better to say to make the Income Tax Act in its application generally more fair. I think that the Income Tax Act is the fairest tax vehicle we have. I think the income tax itself is the fairest tax because it can be applied specifically according to ability to pay and it does not place a heavy burden or a heavier burden upon the poor than upon the rich, not by any means. It is one tax that is hard to hand on. For that reason I support the idea of the income tax, but I do think that all our efforts should be directed towards making its application as fair and just as can possibly be.
Unfortunately, I think that is not done in many instances today. I refer now particularly to the administration of the Income Tax Act, particularly in relation to the farmer taxpayer. I am not going to criticize for a moment some of the things that have already been discussed in this house in another debate such as the net worth statement and all that sort of thing. I am going to talk about the habit of the income tax department of leaving assessments too long and then expecting the farmer taxpayer to feel happy about having to dig up three or four times the amount of tax he thinks he ought to have to pay, and on top of that a penalty or penalties and then to try to put him out of business because he cannot pay immediately when the demand is made.
[Mr. Nicholson.)
I have in mind as an illustration of the thing against which I am complaining, the case of a farmer in western Canada who very faithfully, year after year, put in his income tax returns. He thought, according to his own best calculations, he was paying fair taxes. This went on for years without any complaints or amended assessments coming in from the income tax branch. After several years this man was stunned, almost, to receive from the department of income tax a demand for a very large sum of back taxes. They sent inspectors in to see him. They went over his books most carefully and they did not charge him with having wilfully neglected to pay his fair taxes. They did not suggest at any time the man had withheld taxes. But what they did do was to go back over quite a period of years and assess this man $30,000 of extra taxes, and penalties on top of it, for not having paid.
This man finally said, "Well, all I can do is try to liquidate some of my assets in order to pay." He did start to liquidate and he reduced the arrears and at the same time kept up his current taxes, by something like $18,000. Then, suddenly the department placed the matter in the hands of the exchequer court and got a judgment against him, in spite of the fact every year he had paid $3,000 or $4,000 on these arrears in addition to his current taxes. The exchequer court ruled in favour of the income tax branch and handed down a judgment against the taxpayer. While it is true that they have not yet asked the sheriff to execute the judgment by means of seizures, yet that judgment is hanging over the taxpayer's head. He is not in a position at the moment to liquidate some of his assets because they are tied up in very large holdings and large holdings just do not sell every day or sell easily without being sold at a sacrifice price. The branch, however, is hounding the man and threatening to have the sheriff make a seizure.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in my judgment that is not justice. The man is doing all he can. It has not been proven at any stage that he has wilfully or deliberately attempted to defraud the government of taxes. He is paying as much as he can. He has offered to continue reducing the liability by $3,000 or $4,000 each year in addition to his current taxes, to get it cleaned up. But no, sir, what they want to do is kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. They want to destroy his chance of paying that off by forcing him to sell his assets now at a sacrifice price. This does not give him a chance at all to pay off and to stay in business so he will continue to be a taxpayer. I have seen not only this case but other similar cases and they do not spell justice. It looks

to me as though it is shortsightedness on the part of the officials. I am sure that this case would not be brought to the attention of the minister. I believe that if it were he would take steps to have it corrected. But when we are dealing with the income tax people in these cases they say to us: Now look, we would like to be able to do something on this but we are bound by the act and the regulations under it. This is quite true; they are helpless.
I am, therefore, going to appeal in a general way, not on a specific case but in a general way, to the minister. While we are amending the Income Tax Act, let us make certain that we are doing it in such a manner that the administration of the act can be just to every section of Canadian society. I think that is our responsibility. I think we should always keep in mind that it is far better to have a taxpayer in business continuing to pay taxes than to force him out of business through seizures, judgments and whatnot, and perhaps prevent him from continuing to be a taxpayer. This does not help our situation in Canada one particle. It just shows the rigidity and inhumanity of some of our income tax regulations and the terms of the act. I am going to leave it at that for the moment with the appeal that the government give very serious consideration to that sort of thing to see if they cannot bring in changes in the administration of the act so we can find justice.
The second part of the act in my judgment, Mr. Speaker, is one which permits the federal government to enter into their proposed new tax transfer agreements with the provinces. Those have been negotiated now for quite some time. We think that there are several clauses which should be written in much more general terms than they are. I realize that I would be out of order in referring to specific clauses, and I do not intend to, but in a general way, in this part of the act we think that there are several clauses that are now written in such rigid terms as to hamstring the provinces in their negotiations with the federal government. In view of the fact that no definite arrangements have yet been arrived at between the provinces and the dominion as to these tax transfer arrangements, it looks to me as though-
