I am glad to have that assurance; it just bears out what I was going to say by way of conclusion to this part of my remarks. If you did proceed with them as
Income Tax Act
they are presently written then it might be necessary for the government to come back with another bill amending the Income Tax Act, because the provinces may not agree to the terms under which they are at present written. I just draw that to the attention of the minister for the moment and ask him and his colleagues to look it over most carefully, especially sections 8 and 9, and see if it would not be possible either to leave them over until after the dominion-provincial conference is held or to write them in much more general terms in order to make provision for any changes that might take place in the negotiations when the provinces and the dominion get together.
Aside from those things, Mr. Speaker, I have little which I think should be said at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on second reading of this bill but a few things have come up during the course of this debate on which I should like to comment.
In the first place I should say that under date of June 14, when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) introduced his estimates in this house, I made some remarks which grew out of representations made in the estimates committee and at that time in commenting on my remarks the Minister of National Revenue told me that I appeared to be in the right church but was probably in the wrong pew. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest I am probably in the right pew tonight and I would like to say my prayers all over again, if I may.
There are a few matters on which I should like to remark. First of all I would like to support the plea made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on behalf of self-employed persons who contribute to pension funds on their own behalf. In that regard I draw attention not only to those persons who are in one of the recognized professions but also to those persons who are engaged in business on their own behalf or in partnership. I would like to draw attention to the fact that frequently these people, under extreme hardship to themselves, manage to make contributions to a recognized pension scheme, a scheme which would ordinarily be recognized by the government, had they been employed by others, as an approved or accepted pension scheme or, in the terms of the new bill which is before us, a registered pension scheme and would probably be permitted to deduct from their taxable income the contributions which they make toward the annuity or pension they hope to receive when they are past earning years.

Income Tax Act
These people have no such relief under the law and I think I could do no better than to refer the minister again to the remarks made by the hon. member for Eglin-ton and to those which I made previously on the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue and to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to seriously consider this matter. It is a matter with which I am sure he is familiar; he has had representations made to him by the Canadian tax foundation, the bar association and others, and I trust it will not be too long before he will recognize the just claim of these people.
In the case of consideration of tax returns and appeals made from the assessments pertinent thereto by the income tax department, there are many things that attract the attention of taxpayers.
I recall late last autumn-I think it was in November-reading of a case which had come before the income tax appeal board where a man had supported his mother who was a semi-invalid and had claimed, because of supporting her in a self-contained domestic establishment, the usual $2,000 tax exemption. Then he married and his wife came to live with him and his mother continued to live there and because of the mother's delicate condition of health the wife continued her employment. What transpired was really something that should attract the attention of the Department of Finance because apparently it does not attract the attention of the Department of National Revenue.
This case came before Mr. Commissioner Fisher and in his judgment he pointed out that before marriage the man had been entitled to an exemption on taxable income of $2,000 and his fiancee on her own account had been entitled to an exemption of $1,000. However, after marriage although the wife was still entitled to an exemption of $1,000 by reason of earning more than her statutory exemption, the husband was allowed an exemption of only $1,400. In other words, he was exactly in the same position. He was supporting his mother in the same domestic establishment but his statutory exemption for her was automatically cut from $2,000 to $1,400.
In his judgment Mr. Fisher explained that that is the situation which prevails according to the provisions of the law. Mr. Fisher dwelt upon this matter at some length and pointed out that the evidence showed the man was in receipt of a very modest income and in his unmarried state he came under a
section of the Income Tax Act-and I am quoting from a portion of Mr. Fisher's judgment-which says:
. . . $2,000 may be deducted by a taxpayer who is:
"An unmarried person or a married person not supporting his spouse who maintained a self-contained domestic establishment and actually supported therein a person wholly dependent upon him and connected with him by blood relationship or marriage or adoption."
However, his status changed immediately when he married and instead of having some provision for the income which his wife would have to her credit he found his own statutory exemption was cut by $600.
Then time went on and the mother suffered a severe stroke which left her partly paralysed. The medical expenses mounted and finally they came to the place where, far from the husband supporting his wife, the wife was contributing to the support of her husband and his mother by reason of the illness. Therefore, in his 1953 income tax return this clerk-for such he was- claimed he was not supporting his wife, that she was in fact partly supporting him and therefore he was entitled to the $2,000 deduction. She was paying for the clothes, lodging and food for both but no relief could be given under the act. A report of this judgment appeared in the newspapers and the headline which drew attention to it read, "Couple better off unwed, admits tax board."
Had this woman gone to live with this man in a common-law union and had he continued to support his mother as he had before, he would have been able to claim $2,000 exemption, she could have claimed $1,000 exemption and they would not have suffered financially. But that is not the way we live in Canada. We have respect for our institutions and we have respect for the sanctity of human relations. It seems to me that it is a sorry condition which imposes a penalty on people for observing the moral status which we hope is incumbent upon all of us. I ask the minister to consider the situation which produces these results.
Speaking of marital relations, I should like to refer once more to a matter which was raised earlier this evening by the hon. member for Eglinton, who brought to light again a matter which I brought before this house on June 14 and previously in the committee. This case is known as No. 289 and was heard by the income tax appeal board. It had to do with the payment of alimony by a taxpayer in Ontario under a judgment by the court for the payment of a specific sum. I do not think I can do better than read into the record the words which I read previously. Inasmuch as the current bill gives no recognition to

this problem I am taking the liberty of putting these words once more on the record. In giving his judgment Mr. Fordham had this to say:
Much to the taxpayer's surprise, however, the minister disallowed such deductions-
That is, alimony deductions.
-and ruled that they did not come within the purview of the provision set out above.
That was under section 11 (1) (j).
At the hearing, it became plain that this was because the word "alimony" did not appear after "divorce" in the fourth line of paragraph (j) above. An appeal to the board duly followed.
Then the pertinent words are the following:
The matter reveals for the first time, where the board is concerned, what appears to be a remarkable and unfortunate oversight or omission in the drafting of the foregoing enactment. Although alimony, as such, is clearly deductible by the payer when a court has made an award of alimony in a decree, order or judgment for divorce, or a husband and wife have executed a separation agreement providing for the payment of alimony, subsection (1) (j) does not take cognizance of an action for alimony alone. No reference to such a proceeding is to be found in its wording. Hence, the unfortunate appellant cannot have the relief that is ordinarily afforded to those obligated to pay alimony periodically. The words "judicial separation" do not assist him, as the Ontario courts are without jurisdiction to entertain actions for judicial separation.
I am not a lawyer and I recall quite well that when I quoted those words previously the minister expressed some surprise and shook his head at hearing my quotation. However, I have inquired into the matter since then and I understand that there is no such thing legally as a judicial separation in the courts of Ontario. I thought that probably somebody had made a mistake when the minister shook his head on the previous occasion and I tried to find out just what the situation was. The legal niceties escape me, I admit, but I find that Mr. Fordham was quite correct and that there is actually no such thing in Ontario.
It would seem to me that in the drafting of this act those who had charge of the wording overlooked the fact that Ontario was in this position. It seems to me that because of that persons in Ontario who are caught under these provisions are at a disadvantage as compared with persons in other provinces. I once more ask the minister if he will please do something about this situation. It seems to me to be grossly unfair that a man who accepts responsibility of caring for the family he has undertaken to care for should not have the advantage of deducting from his taxable income the money which he expends in this way. Those persons who go through the normal course of divorce proceedings and are thereby free to engage in other marital connections in the future are placed in a different
Income Tax Act
position from this woman, who has no desire to do other than live apart and is thus circumscribed by the law from having the advantage of deducting for income tax purposes her living expenses.
There are a couple of other things which I feel constrained to put before the house on this occasion because previously I inadvertently got into the wrong pew. One is the matter of rental income which accrues to the benefit of an individual through the hands of an executor or trustee. Once more I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and the house because it is only a short time ago that the minister in bringing down some of his regulations-it escapes me whether it was in the budget or subsequently-exempted from surtax on investment income revenue derived from rental property. Under the conditions set out for estates and trusts in the T3 form under the section headed "Tax on Income in Hands of Executor or Trustee" appears a note reading as follows:
Rental income from real property and income from a business or farm operated by the executor or trustee are not subject to surtax in his hands.
Yet when these funds eventually are reported by the beneficiary as income he pays a surtax as investment income, largely by reason of the fact that there is no other place to record this income on the ordinary T1 form other than income received as investment income from estates and trusts.
As I said on a former occasion, the courts have several times, and almost invariably, ruled that income should not change its character by reason of passing from a source through a trustee to a beneficiary. Yet under our own income tax law, regardless of the law set out, the regulations in effect in the income tax department prohibit the taxpayer from claiming this income as earned income despite the fact that persons who have rental income on their own account and who receive it first-hand are able to claim it as earned income.
I recognize that this is a fairly recent concession of the department, that is, the concession given to the individual to claim rental income as earned income, and it may mean that the minister has not yet got around to allowing this same concession where the funds come to the individual through an estate or trust. But once more-this time I am in the right pew-I ask the minister to seriously consider this matter and to bring in the necessary amendment to the act if it requires that or, if not-and the latter is my view-simply instruct the department to make the necessary correction to the T1 form, which will place the income from revenue, even though coming to the taxpayer through an estate or trust, in the earned income bracket.

Income Tax Act
I suggest to the minister that it is as simple as that: a change in the printing of the T1 form. I do not believe it is a matter that requires an amendment to the act. The minister himself brought in this amendment a few years ago, and I think it is merely an oversight that could be readily rectified by changing the T3 and T1 forms so that the two categories of income, that is, from dividends or other investments and from rental income, be reported separately and be reported by the ultimate beneficiary in two separate brackets on his own income tax return. I ask the minister seriously if he will look into that matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) will permit me, I should like to ask the house for a little assistance. We are on the second reading of a bill and we are supposed to be discussing the principle of the bill. I realize that this bill is a collection of disconnected amendments dealing with such subjects as railway companies, oil companies, solicitor-client privilege, pensions funds and so on, and may not be said to have any specific principle, but I must ask the house not to use this bill as a vehicle for every conceivable form of criticism or suggestion of and to the Departments of National Revenue and Finance, because there are a great many aspects of our taxation which are not included in this bill. The last thing I want to do is to make it difficult for any member to put forward his views, but I think perhaps at this time I should say that there may come a time when it will be necessary to say, "That is a little beyond the scope of this bill."

I think it has been the custom of those who have preceded me to talk not about the particular clauses in this bill but about the particular clauses which are not in this bill and which should be. Before you pronounced your admonition, Mr. Speaker, I was going to do the same thing. I think I shall venture, in view of your kind remarks at the conclusion, to do just that, and I hope that the warning will have some effect upon my more immediate or less immediate neighbours. Of course, one has to draw the line somewhere.
There are one or two things about which I am disappointed in this act in that they are not mentioned in the act. One has to do with charitable donations. I think that what I am going to speak about can be defined as charitable donations. This is perhaps particularly applicable to my own province of Saskatchewan, where we at least think, whatever may be the opinion of those in other provinces, that we have adhered to our program of humanities first and that we

are in the lead in proportion to our population in the providing of decent living conditions for our older citizens. To do that costs money. We have to receive gifts-and I consider them charitable donations-in order to get the first payment for these propositions. Service clubs, churches and people who interest themselves in this sort of thing go out and ask people for money. The very first question they are asked is, "Are these payments deductible as charitable donations?" We have to tell them'that under the present law they are not.
I was very much astonished that when this was mentioned the other day here in the house, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott)-I hope he did not mean it; I hope he was joking-said, "Why don't you just give it as a church subscription, and then it would be automatically deducted." As far as I am concerned, for me to do that would be dishonest. I do not know what it would be for my hon. friend. If I give a donation on the basis of a private payment for the building of an old people's home, I do not think that that is, after all, a church subscription. I know that that sort of thing is done. However, I have said enough about that, but I think that those payments should be deductible. I cannot see any difference between those and regular charitable donations.
Another matter about which I should like to say a word is the ceiling upon the old age pension payments. Of course, members and, I think, most of the public, are aware that we have to pay extra tax, as we should, to provide ourselves and others with old age pensions: 2 per cent extra on the taxable income. In other words, if I have a taxable income of $1,000, I pay 2 per cent extra or $20 extra for old age pension purposes. If I have $2,000 income, I pay 2 per cent or $40. If I have $3,000 taxable income, I pay 2 per cent extra or $60. But then- and it is a strange thing to me-at that point the schedule ceases to exist. From then on, irrespective of the size of my taxable income, I pay $60 only.
To me there is no justice in that; there could not be to one who thinks of things as I do. If a man has a taxable income of $10,000 or $15,000, he has to contribute only $60 from the wealth with which he has been blessed to help pay for the pensions of those who are not so able. I think something should be done about that. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) should let that scale slide. I am thinking of a sliding scale. Let it slide. Let it keep on sliding.
Another thing I want to bring up is the matter of corporation profits. I have to confess to having two small investments in

Canadian corporations and they bring me in a total of approximately $40 a year. I discover that at the end of the year I am allowed to deduct one-fifth of that $40 not from the amount of money upon which my income tax is based, but from the actual tax itself after the tax is computed. I can see no reason or justice in that. I can see no reason why I should be allowed to deduct $8 from the actual amount of tax which I otherwise would have had to pay if I did not have these investments. I know that what I am going to say now has been disputed. I do not think it has been disputed in this house because I know it can not be disputed. I do not know what the exact figures are but let us say that a man has an income somewhere between $10,000 and $11,000. I see the minister is getting ready to interrupt. He has heard this mathematical formula before.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We have heard it every year.

You are going to hear it a lot more and as far as I am concerned the people throughout the country are going to keep on hearing it too. May I say to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) that audiences are so aghast when they hear this that they simply do not believe that even this Liberal government could perpetrate such a thing.
They will from now on.

It is a fact that if a man is working as a doctor, a top mechanic or whatever you like, earns somewhere between $10,000 and $11,000 by so working and has a wife and a couple of children if he is a normal man, he discovers that he has to pay income tax of about $1,600. I say "about". I am getting away from pure mathematics. But if that same man were in the position where he had never done a tap of work in his life but had an income of between $10,000 and $11,000 a year from investments in Canadian corporations his income tax would be exactly nil. That is a word that has been introduced by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and this is another nil. The amount of income tax he would pay would be exactly nil except for the aforesaid $60 that he would have to pay on account of the old age pension. If the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue, who was good enough to interject, can deny that statement, let them get up and deny it now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Do you take into account that the income he has has probably come from
Income Tax Act
corporations which pay 47 per cent on it before he ever gets it?
I am very well aware of the argument that the corporation funds have already been taxed in the hands of the corporation. That is that old thing I have heard so often before.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: So is yours old.

The minister will tell me that it is double taxation but the government is not so particular about double taxation being perpetrated in certain other directions which, if I had the time, I could mention here. But what I have stated is largely, if not mathematically, accurate and true. It is true, and to me it is a disgrace and a blot on our national life. Any government that can perpetrate that sort of thing or that would believe that sort of thing is right has an attitude towards things and people in which I cannot share. I know the argument is put forward that we want to encourage Canadian investment. There are other ways. We do not have to encourage it to that extent, to that degree or by that method.
As I have said, the people do not believe it. I said it once before in an election campaign and somebody wrote a letter to the Star-Phoenix and said: "This man Knight should not be allowed to go around telling lies. The thing is impossible, the thing is ridiculous. Of course anybody with an income of $10,000 has to pay a proportionate amount to the national treasury." Well, I countered that statement. I took an income tax form and went down to my hon. friend's department. I told them that I wanted the income tax form filled out in the name of Brown, Smith, Jones or whatever you like. They said, "What are the conditions?" I gave them the conditions. I gave them a hypothetical case. I put the income at $11,000 or $12,000 and said that the man had a wife and two children and was such and such an age. I told them I wanted to know what his income tax would be.
They asked from where the man derived his income. I gave them the names of certain Canadian corporations. I said, "I want you to fill that out and fill it out right because I am going to ask you to sign it when you have finished." The man laughed. I presume he knew what I was after. However, he did his work. I will say that for him. He filled it out and he said that the man would ordinarily pay income tax of $1,600 or $1,700 but because of the fact that he derived his income from dividends from Canadian corporations solely the only thing he would have to pay would be $60 towards the old age pension inasmuch he would have an exemption of 20

Income Tax Act
per cent or $2,000 on the $10,000 he received in dividends. I said, "Would you please fill that out and sign it?" He did so. I then went and took a quarter page in the paper as a paid advertisement, and they did not call me a liar after that.
I suggest that the minister look into that matter. It is iniquitous, unfair and unjust, no matter how you look at it. The Minister of National Revenue was talking about double taxation. I wish we could get some proper definition of what they are now beginning to call under the act, and I am referring to the act, "registered pension funds" because there is a considerable amount of confusion in that regard. I receive letters about it all the time and I am sure that other members do too. Let us take what used to be my own profession, teaching. Here we have a superannuation fund which we create. The province of Saskatchewan puts in so much, we put in so much and so on, and after a while you get a pension. In their innocence these people said that it would be fine if anybody wanted to pay in more than the amount that was called for. It would be a form of extra saving, and a lot of people put in a little extra money, $1,000 or $1,500, over the course of a good many years. But when they come to take the money out it is a different proposition. You take it out and you pay income tax on it.
We paid income tax on the money as we earned it, but when we put it in the fund it suddenly became engulfed in this lack of definition of what is properly a registered pension fund. Is it a savings bank? Is it a benevolent society, or what is it? Before we are through it may be a small loan company. At any rate, there is some doubt about the matter. When you go to take out your money and get back the money you put in you are told you have to pay income tax on it for the second time. That is what I meant when I reminded the Minister of National Revenue that in some cases they do not worry too much about double taxation.
The same question has arisen with regard to other provisions and other societies of one sort and another. I think the last letter I had was from a group of firemen in the city of Saskatoon. Because of some little technicality the department had decided that they were not operating what is called a registered pension fund.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) referred to the need of people who do not .pay income tax at all. I should like to say a word or two on behalf of those who have sufficient income to just pay income tax, and I shall be brief. I do not want to shut somebody else off. I shall simply say that I think these income tax exemptions

should be raised in view of our present prosperity. We hear a great deal about it from the government side. We hear about the increase in the gross national product, how well we are doing, how our surpluses are climbing. I think this is probably a direction in which these smaller people should get some help. I am all for the income tax. I think it is a good, fair and just method of taxation. However, I think there are some people now paying income tax who should not be paying it at all.
There is another thing I wish to mention and with this I conclude. I hope that this bill will provide for this point. The minister can inform me whether or not it does so. I am thinking particularly of farmers. I am not so clear about the matter of labour unions. I have not studied the matter. I am thinking of the business of conventions. Certainly I think that people who are gathered together in farm unions should be allowed to deduct the expenses of their conventions. I see the minister nodding his head although that does not appear in Hansard. I am asking the minister now whether it is true that, by a clause in this bill, from now on those farmers who attend farm union conventions will be allowed to deduct their expenses for income tax purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is one provision which may not be as wide as my hon. friend has suggested. However, there is a provision. We can discuss it in committee of the whole.

When we come to committee of the whole I also want to ask my hon. friend what the situation is with regard to labour unions in the matter of attending conventions. I want to know whether that will come under the same heading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It does.
With those few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I think I will leave the matter until the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I shall try to remain within the confines of this bill. Although you may think that I am somewhat remotely within the confines of it, I think that I am within the terms of the bill, at least as much as were some hon. members who have spoken previously. I was afraid that my friend the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), having been a high school principal for many years and being an educationalist, was perhaps going to steal or, shall I say,-
Borrow?
-expropriate some of my material.
He wants good material.

I want to bring to the minister's attention something that is lacking in respect of this income tax bill. After all, we always have an income tax bill which in the main revamps the income tax system of the country. I refer now to the fact that there is no exemption whatsoever for the taxpayer who supports a son or daughter who is going to university. A change was made in the Income Tax Act some years ago and at that time I was certainly under the impression that exemptions were allowed on behalf of income tax payers who supported their young people as they went through university. However, my eyes were opened when I found that it was necessary for me to support my young lad. It is a strange thing to me that this matter has escaped me over the years but, according to the Income Tax Act, if an income tax payer claims exemption for himself and his wife, he cannot claim exemption for a son or a daughter who is dependent upon him for his or her university education. To me that is a serious matter. A farmer, for instance, might raise hogs, cattle or something else. He is allowed to write off certain operating expenses as he raises those hogs and cattle. But here is a man who raises a family. It is granted that he gets the family allowance while his children are young. But the moment they come of age where they wear bigger shoes, eat like a horse, wear men's clothes and when the young daughters are obliged to wear more expensive clothes, he cannot claim exemption for them. It is all right if they are forced onto the labour market and earn their own living, but if they want to go forward to a higher school of learning such as a university and prepare to be an engineer or a doctor, the old man must foot the bill. I maintain that is not fair or right. I assert that the Income Tax Act should be amended in order to allow an exemption for a young man or a ypung woman going to university. Otherwise only the people who are in the higher income brackets will be able to afford to put their young people through university. People with moderate incomes just cannot afford to put a young man or young woman through university.
I calculate that it takes about $1,000 a year, even though the young man or the young woman may earn a certain amount of money during summer vacations. It costs a great deal to put a young man or young woman through university. There is the matter of clothes to wear and certain upkeep including board, fraternity fees, tuition and books. It costs a great deal of money. As a matter of fact, if the young person is not earning an income, we are allowed $400 67509-358
Income Tax Act
exemption for him or her but we are allowed that anyway when they get to a certain age, provided they are still going to school. But as soon as they graduate from high school and want to go to university we are then allowed the same exemption of only $400. That simply means this, Mr. Speaker. As soon as they arrive at the age where they are able to go to university, then there is no exemption from the income tax at all and no assistance whatsoever. I believe that the minister should take that matter into consideration and permit the $1,000 income tax exemption that is allowed. Here is where the discrepancy comes in. If a man does not have a wife, and manages to get along without one, he can send his boy to university and claim $1,000 exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Where would he get the boy if he has no wife?

But if he is married and has a wife to look after the home, he cannot claim that exemption. If he has a housekeeper to look after his home, he can claim exemption for her if he happens to be a widower, but he cannot claim exemption for his son. You cannot claim more than $1,000 for either a wife, a housekeeper or a son or daughter who is going to university. Now, that seems to me to be unfair. It seems to me to be ridiculous. I would ask the minister to give some real consideration to the amendment of the Income Tax Act so that some further exemption could be allowed to the people who are putting their sons and daughters through university.

The
minister whose bill we are discussing has been quite frank in his acknowledgement about the rate of income tax and taxation generally in Canada. He, like everyone else, appreciates that we are living in an age of high taxation and has expressed himself from time to time as being concerned with relief from that high rate of taxation. He is equally frank, I think, in introducing this bill by saying that this does not to any extent relieve the Canadian payers of income tax from taxation. I think the major relief from taxation referred to in the budget is in another field.
Now, the problem of the rate of taxation is one that is frequently discussed and presented to the government. I think the words used by the Canadian Tax Foundation express about as succinctly as possible what I have in mind. They say:
The growth of social welfare expenses and defence spending has brought about in the past 15 years an unprecedented level of expenditures in relation to national income, and rates of taxation are very high today by previous peacetime standards.

Income Tax Act
Now, that is undoubtedly so, and apparently in the view of the government is to remain so at least for another year. In bringing in a bill of this kind it seems to me that, without dealing with the rate of taxation at great length or without dealing with the rate at all, there are a number of amendments by way of exemption and alteration which could be made which would improve the taxation system and give an incentive here and a disincentive, if I may use such a horrible word, in other places, or increase the social justice, if you like, of the tax system. I suppose the minister, in bringing forward most of these amendments, is making some corrections of one kind or another, removing an anomaly here and giving an incentive there. From that point of view one cannot complain too greatly about the contents of the bill. As has been said by other speakers, the complaint is rather about what is omitted from than what is contained in the bill. There are a great many moderate incentive provisions which have been suggested from time to time, which would not be costly and which would not affect the over-all rates but would achieve a very definite end in themselves.
I know this applies not only to the field of trade and commerce in the broad sense, that is the economy in the sense of its industrial progress, but also in the personal field to the individual in his daily occupation. We have had two or three specific examples of the kind of thing that might have been considered. I realize that the use of the income tax in the larger field of providing incentive in trade is a very important one and could be the subject of a very lengthy debate. I think, however, perhaps this is not the appropriate bill upon which to enter that field. I just illustrate the kind of thing I mean by drawing the minister's attention to the effect of taxation in certain fields as presented by the tax foundation recently in making a presentation to the royal commission. They dealt with the effect of taxation on the development of natural resources, for example; on fixed capital expenditure; on exports and so on over the broad field of the economy. As I say, that might better be discussed at another time, although it is of prime importance and deserves the attention of this house, particularly in some of the fields which have been brought to the attention of the house this session. For example, there is the encouragement of Canadians to invest on equal terms with foreign investors in the development of their own country.
I shall refer briefly to the incentives which affect the individual more directly, two or three of them. Before giving an example of that, I should like to say that this bill might
[Mr. Michener.l
very properly be brought before a committee because there are a good many minor matters which will only be incorporated in legislation of this kind and discussed fully in a special committee such as the committee on banking and commerce. There is not much opportunity in the committee of the whole house to move minor amendments to try to patch up various inconsistencies and injustices of the present tax law. The suggestion which has been made to refer the bill to a committee seems to me to have a great deal of merit, just to deal with what I might call incidentals, odds and ends of amendments which have escaped the minister's attention.
The first example I wish to bring to his attention is that of the allowance made for children. There is a case where our tax system seems to compare unfavourably with tax systems elsewhere. As recently as last May a public comparison was made of our attitude in this respect with that of the United Kingdom as shown by the new income tax tables made effective in Britain at that time. When compared to those in this country they showed that although income taxes are higher there than they are here, they grant much more consideration to parents than Canadian income tax laws do.
The Globe and Mail of May 4, in its editorial, had this to say in one paragraph:
Taking family allowances (paid in both countries) into account, it can be seen that at every level from $2,000 a year-$40 a week-up, British parents enjoy a substantially greater advantage in relation to non-parents than do their Canadian counterparts. Westminster, in short, would appear to have more respect for the family life, and its accompanying expenses, than Ottawa.
An example of that, I think, is the way allowances for children and the family allowance can operate where a child is born towards the end of the year. A father who pays taxes and has been blessed with another child in December is allowed the exemption of $150 from his taxable income.
